after.headline: After an overdose
after.intro: Surviving an overdose is not the end of it. This is what tends to happen next — in a body, in a head, and between people — for whoever it happened to and whoever was in the room. Nothing here asks anyone to change anything.

survivor.title: If it was you
survivor.intro: You are probably being handled right now — by people who are frightened, or relieved, or angry at you for scaring them. Here is the part nobody sits down and explains.

window.title: The next few hours are the risky part
window.body: Naloxone wears off after 30 to 90 minutes. Most opioids keep working for longer than that — methadone for many hours — so it is possible to be brought back and then go under again as the naloxone leaves before the drug does. This is not a rare thing and it is not a sign anything was done wrong.
window.detail: Federal guidance is that someone stays with you for at least four hours from the last dose of naloxone. If nobody can stay, be with someone who has naloxone on hand. If you use again in that window, the naloxone already in you may blunt it — and people have taken more to get past that, which is how the four hours turn dangerous.

sources.name: SAMHSA Overdose Prevention and Response Toolkit (2023)

watch.title: What to watch for, and when
watch.intro: Some of this shows up days later, long after everyone has decided you are fine. None of it is likely. All of it is worth knowing so you are not talking yourself out of getting seen.

items.what: Breathing slowing, getting hard to wake, lips or fingertips going blue or gray.
items.when: First 30 to 90 minutes, as the naloxone wears off

items.sign: Breathing that stays bad after you have come to
items.what: Short of breath when the drug has clearly worn off, sometimes coughing up pink frothy spit. Fluid in the lungs is a known thing after an opioid overdose.

items.sign: A chest infection that arrives late
items.what: Fever, a cough, fast breathing, wheezing, a racing heart. If you threw up or were face-down while you were out, some of it can get into the lungs and turn into an infection well after you feel better.
items.when: 48 to 72 hours later — the one people miss

items.sign: A limb that hurts far too much
items.what: Pain out of proportion to anything you did, tightness or swelling, numbness — usually where your body weight was resting while you were out. Muscle can be crushed by nothing more than lying still for hours, and it can damage the kidneys.
items.when: Hours to days. If a limb is tight, badly painful or numb, that is an emergency now — treatment inside six hours is what protects the limb.

items.what: Dark, red or cola-colored urine, or passing very little, along with muscle pain, aching or weakness.
items.when: Clear urine does NOT mean you are fine — the classic combination shows up in fewer than half of cases, so go by the muscle pain.

watch.note: None of this needs a diagnosis from you. It needs you to mention that you overdosed when you get seen, because it changes what they look for.

sources.name: Merck Manual — aspiration pneumonitis and pneumonia

risk.title: The honest number
risk.body: Of 11,557 people treated in Massachusetts emergency departments for a non-fatal opioid overdose, 5.5% died within a year, 1.1% within a month, and 0.25% within two days. The first month — and especially the first two days — is the most dangerous stretch.
risk.detail: That is a real risk and it is also a survivable one: the overwhelming majority of those people were alive a year later. It is here because the days right after are exactly when people assume the danger has passed, and because if there was ever a week to not use alone, it is this one.

sources.name: Weiner et al., Annals of Emergency Medicine (2020)

brain.title: About your head
brain.body: Among 205 emergency department visits for fentanyl overdose in one US hospital system, 14% of people were diagnosed with encephalopathy or anoxic brain injury and 20% reported memory loss afterwards. Those are people whose overdose brought them to an emergency department, not everyone who overdoses.
brain.detail: If you are foggy, losing words, or cannot remember the day, that is worth telling a doctor and it is not proof of permanent damage. A review of 79 studies found outcomes running the whole range from full recovery to lasting problems, and no one can currently give you a number. Fluid on the lungs, for its part, cleared within a day in about three quarters of cases and within two days in the rest — though a third of that group needed a breathing machine first.

sources.name: Fentanyl overdose ED outcomes, Drug and Alcohol Dependence Reports
Hypoxic brain injury review, J Neurological Sciences (2022)

items.t: If you woke up furious, that is not a character flaw
items.b: Being brought back with naloxone can drop you straight into withdrawal, and people often come to sick, exposed, and surrounded by an audience. Anger in that moment is one of the most normal reactions there is.

items.t: You may be treated differently now
items.b: People who were casual with you may start watching you. Some of that is love wearing a bad expression. It is still exhausting, and you are allowed to find it exhausting.

items.t: You do not owe anyone a transformation
items.b: Surviving an overdose is the moment everyone expects a decision. You can make one. You can also not, and come back to this page in a year, and that is a legitimate way to use it.

items.t: Being ashamed is common and it is not a reason to stay away from care
items.b: Plenty of people avoid a follow-up because they cannot face the conversation. If that is you, the physical things above are the reason to go anyway — you can decline every other conversation on offer.

items.t: Your tolerance is not what it was
items.b: If you spent time in a hospital, a cell, or detox — anywhere you used less or not at all — the amount that was normal before is now enough to stop your breathing. This is the single most common way people die after surviving.

survivor.closing: If you want naloxone of your own so this does not depend on whoever happens to be nearby, Learn has where to get it free.

witness.title: If you were there
witness.intro: You may have done rescue breathing on someone you love, or found them a color you will not forget. Almost nothing is written for you.

anger.title: If they woke up angry at you
anger.body: This is the part that makes people swear they will never do it again — and there is research on it that almost nobody has heard. In a study of 47 overdose reversals by trained bystanders in New York City, anger afterwards was strongly tied to how the responder spoke to the person, not to whether they were in withdrawal. The researchers found no evidence that people with withdrawal symptoms were any more likely to be angry.
anger.detail: What helped: talking to them, explaining what had happened, trying to calm them. What made it much worse: criticizing, scolding, or reacting angrily when they were upset. So if it went badly it was not because you saved them, and next time there is something you can actually do — tell them what happened and stay gentle, even though your own adrenaline is screaming.

sources.name: Neale et al., J Substance Abuse Treatment (2020)

items.t: The images come back
items.b: Seeing it again when you are trying to sleep, checking on them more than you need to, jolting at the sound of a door. This is what a nervous system does after a thing like that. It usually settles.

items.t: You were probably angry at them while you were saving them
items.b: People report this constantly and almost never say it out loud, because it feels monstrous. It is not. You can be terrified for someone and furious at them in the same minute.

items.t: You should not be the only one holding this
items.b: If you are the person who always has the naloxone, the one who checks, the one who answers at 3am — that is a real weight and it does not lift because you love them. Train one more person. Two people who know what to do is better than one who never gets to be off duty.

items.t: You did not cause it and you cannot guarantee the next one
items.b: The instinct afterwards is to work out what you should have noticed. There is often nothing. The supply is inconsistent in ways nobody in the room can see.

items.t: More naloxone is not better naloxone
items.b: In one CDC study of 354 police administrations, people given 8 mg of nasal naloxone were about two and a half times as likely to go into withdrawal as those given 4 mg, with survival essentially identical. Give a dose, wait, give another if breathing has not improved. The goal is breathing, not consciousness.

grief.title: If they died
grief.body: Overdose grief is not harder than grief after a suicide — research comparing the two keeps finding they sit at about the same place, including for stigma, guilt and shame. Both are considerably harder than losing someone to an accident or to illness. If you feel like people are treating this death as different, as somehow less deserving of casseroles and cards, you are not imagining it and it is not a fair reading of your person. There are people below who lost someone the same way.

substances.name: Xylazine
substances.summary: A veterinary sedative, not an opioid. It is almost always found mixed into fentanyl rather than sold on its own.

whyInSupply.text: Added deliberately. Sources document two motives and do not agree on which dominates: to extend or change the effect of fentanyl, and to add weight cheaply. Some people seek it out to lengthen a short fentanyl high; others describe it as something they did not want in their supply.

sources.name: CDC — What you should know about xylazine

naloxone.lead: Naloxone does not reverse xylazine — give it anyway.
naloxone.text: Xylazine is not an opioid, so naloxone does nothing to it. But it is nearly always mixed with fentanyl, and naloxone reverses that. CDC guidance is to give naloxone in any suspected overdose. Expect the person to stay sedated after naloxone works: that is the xylazine, not a failed dose, and it is not a reason to keep giving more.

sources.name: CDC — What you should know about xylazine

overdose.title: Rescue breathing matters more here
overdose.body: Xylazine slows breathing on its own, and CDC specifically notes rescue breaths are especially helpful after xylazine. Tilt the head back, pinch the nose, give two slow breaths, then one breath every five seconds.

overdose.title: Recovery position, and stay
overdose.body: Roll the person onto their side so they do not choke if they vomit. Sedation can outlast the naloxone, so staying with them matters more than usual.

effects.title: Wounds — and what they actually are
effects.body: Xylazine is associated with severe skin wounds. They are not caused by a flesh-eating infection, whatever the news calls it: the leading explanation is that blood vessels constrict and tissue is starved of blood. Health officials say the cause is still not well understood. Wounds can appear anywhere on the body, away from any injection site, and regardless of whether someone injects, smokes, or snorts.

sources.name: Philadelphia DPH — Caring for people with xylazine-associated wounds

effects.title: Basic wound care you can do yourself
effects.body: Clean with saline, or soap and water. Apply a petroleum-based ointment and keep the wound bed moist — dry wounds do not heal. Cover with a two-layer dressing. Do not use alcohol or peroxide: they kill human cells and dry the wound out.

effects.title: When a wound needs a clinician
effects.body: Exposed bone or tendon, not being able to move a joint, fever, unexplained nausea or vomiting, confusion, pus, swelling, a smell that remains after cleaning, increasing pain, redness or warmth. Using drugs is not a reason to be refused wound care, and health departments say so explicitly.

withdrawal.text: Not established. Clinicians suspect a xylazine withdrawal syndrome exists, but as of current health department guidance it is not a defined syndrome, and one 2025 study of 71 patients found no measurable difference in withdrawal scores between people whose tests showed xylazine and those with fentanyl alone. Treat claims of a distinct, severe xylazine withdrawal with caution — the evidence is not there yet. This is not the case for medetomidine.

detection.text: Xylazine test strips exist and are widely given out free. They miss a lot. In one Los Angeles study of 333 fentanyl-positive samples the strips caught under half of the xylazine that was actually there, with misses concentrated in samples containing small amounts. Lidocaine can produce a false positive. A negative strip does not mean there is no xylazine.

sources.name: Test strip field performance, Los Angeles

prevalence.text: Regional, and changing fast. Across 32 jurisdictions in 2021–22, xylazine was detected in 9% of deaths involving illegally made fentanyl — but that ranged from about 28% in Maryland down to roughly 1% of such deaths in the entire West. It is also now falling in the place it was most common: Philadelphia drug checking found xylazine in 97% of fentanyl samples in early 2024 and 21% by late 2025, as medetomidine replaced it. Testing for xylazine is inconsistent between jurisdictions, so counts understate it.

sources.name: CDC MMWR — Xylazine in IMF-involved deaths

substances.name: Medetomidine
substances.summary: Another veterinary sedative from the same family as xylazine, but far stronger and longer-lasting. It has largely replaced xylazine in some cities.

whyInSupply.text: Found mixed into illegally made fentanyl. Where it comes from is not established — researchers list diverted veterinary product, diverted human hospital sedative, and illicit synthesis as possibilities without settling between them. No source establishes a motive, so this page does not offer one.

naloxone.lead: Naloxone does not reverse medetomidine — give it anyway, and check breathing first.
naloxone.text: Medetomidine is not an opioid. Naloxone will not touch it, but it reverses the fentanyl it is mixed with, so give it. Health departments have changed the order of the steps because of medetomidine: check whether the person is BREATHING before checking whether they respond to you. Someone can be breathing adequately and still be completely unresponsive from medetomidine, and checking responsiveness first misleads you into thinking naloxone has not worked.

sources.name: PA Department of Health HAN #794 (relaying Philadelphia DPH)

overdose.title: Smaller naloxone doses are preferred
overdose.body: State guidance now prefers low-dose naloxone here — enough to restore breathing, no more. Large doses can throw someone into the severe withdrawal described below, which is itself dangerous.

overdose.title: Expect sedation to last a long time
overdose.body: Medetomidine outlasts both naloxone and xylazine. If the person is lying down, put them in the recovery position. If they are sitting, tilt their head back and to the side so their airway stays open. Check nothing is trapping their arms or legs. Stay with them until they come to.

effects.title: It does not appear to cause wounds
effects.body: Worth saying plainly, because people reasonably assume it behaves like xylazine. Health officials state medetomidine has not been shown to cause wounds, and Philadelphia saw wound-related presentations fall by roughly half after medetomidine entered its supply.

effects.title: How much stronger than xylazine
effects.body: Sources disagree. Health departments say 100–200 times; a 2026 research paper says 200–300 times. Both trace back to the same 1988 pharmacology study. What they agree on is that it is far stronger and lasts longer.

withdrawal.text: This is well documented and it is dangerous. Of 165 people hospitalized in Philadelphia between September 2024 and January 2025, 91% needed intensive care and 24% needed a breathing tube. It presents as a racing heart and very high blood pressure, sweating, tremor, nausea, restlessness, and alertness that comes and goes. It resists the usual treatments — opioids, benzodiazepines and clonidine — and most people responded to dexmedetomidine instead. It can begin within hours of last use and peaks around 18 to 36 hours. It can be triggered by receiving naloxone. If you are withdrawing and your heart is racing and your blood pressure is high, this is a reason to get to a hospital.

detection.text: Medetomidine strips became available during 2025 — older guidance saying no test exists is out of date. They have a specific quirk: the drug comes in two mirror-image forms, and some strip lots only react to one of them, so a negative can be wrong depending on which form is present and which lot you have. Detomidine, another veterinary sedative, sets them off falsely, and so can levamisole. Xylazine does not cross-react.

prevalence.text: Heavily concentrated in the Northeast and close to absent in the West. CDC drug-checking across 20 sites in late 2025 found medetomidine in about 74% of opioid-positive samples in the Northeast, 56% in the Midwest, 30% in the South, and under 4% in the West. In Philadelphia it went from absent in early 2024 to 88% of fentanyl samples by late 2025. Where you are matters more for this substance than for almost anything else on this app.

substances.nameNote: Dexmedetomidine is not another name for this. It is the mirror-image form, sold as Precedex, and it is a licensed hospital sedative — one of the things used to treat medetomidine withdrawal. Street samples tested so far have all been the racemic form.

substances.name: Nitazenes
substances.summary: A family of synthetic opioids never approved for medical use anywhere. Unlike xylazine and medetomidine, these ARE opioids — so naloxone works on them.

whyInSupply.text: Sold as opioids in their own right and also found mixed into other drugs. They were first made about sixty years ago as candidate painkillers and were never approved. Why they appear where they do is not well characterized, and this page does not guess.

naloxone.lead: Naloxone works on nitazenes at normal doses.
naloxone.text: You may have read that nitazenes need many times the usual amount of naloxone. The published evidence does not support that. A 2025 review found a median effective dose of about 1.2 mg, and under 1 mg when given before reaching hospital — ordinary doses. Some people need a second dose, as with any strong opioid. The genuine difference is duration: the nitazene can outlast the naloxone, so someone can wake up and then go back under. Stay with them, and call 911 even if they seem fine.

overdose.title: Do not leave after they wake up
overdose.body: The most important difference with nitazenes is how long they last. In one review, some cases needed naloxone kept running continuously because the opioid effect persisted. Naloxone wearing off before the drug does is the specific thing to watch for: breathing can stop again after everyone in the room has relaxed. Stay with them.

effects.title: On strength claims
effects.body: "Hundreds of times stronger than fentanyl" is true of some members of this family in laboratory tests and not true of the family as a whole — CDC notes metonitazene's potency is similar to fentanyl's. Researchers also note that real-world potency often comes out lower than lab figures, and that human data is scarce.

detection.text: Nitazene strips have been sold since early 2024. A laboratory evaluation found they picked up 24 of 33 nitazenes tested, and needed a fairly large amount present to react. The consistent blind spot is a related group called desnitazenes, which the strips are not built to catch. The researchers put it plainly: a negative result does not mean a sample is safe. The strips also cannot tell you which nitazene it is or how much.

prevalence.text: Rising, and still numerically small. Tennessee recorded no nitazene-involved deaths in 2019, 10 in 2020 and 42 in 2021. Nationally, confirmed nitazene-involved deaths number in the hundreds per year against roughly 80,000 overdose deaths overall in 2024. Two things are true at once: this is a small share of deaths, and it is genuinely undercounted, because few laboratories test for nitazenes at all. Mid-Atlantic drug checking found none at all in late 2025.

substances.name: BTMPS
substances.summary: An industrial chemical used to stop plastic degrading in sunlight. It is not a drug, has never been studied in people, and began appearing in the fentanyl supply in 2024.

whyInSupply.text: Nobody knows. Researchers offer two possibilities — a change in how fentanyl is being made, or simple dilution — and explicitly decline to choose between them. Samples containing BTMPS did have less fentanyl in them, which fits the dilution idea without proving it.

naloxone.lead: Unknown — respond as you would to any opioid overdose.
naloxone.text: Health officials say plainly that it is not known how BTMPS affects overdose risk. Because it turns up alongside fentanyl, the guidance is the standard one: give naloxone, give rescue breaths between doses if they are not breathing, stop once they are breathing on their own, use the recovery position if they stay sedated, and call 911.

effects.title: There is no human research at all
effects.body: Health officials state there are no studies of BTMPS use in people. What exists is animal data showing heart toxicity and eye damage. People who have encountered it report ringing ears, blurred vision and a taste like plastic or bug spray when smoking it, and burning when injecting — these are self-reports, not clinical findings.

detection.text: There is no test strip for BTMPS. Finding it requires laboratory equipment, which in practice means a drug-checking service rather than anything you can do yourself.

prevalence.text: Uncertain, and falling where it was measured. A study across nine US locations in 2024 found BTMPS in about a third of drug samples from Los Angeles and Philadelphia. Philadelphia's health department published its own figures of 16% and 11% in June and July 2024, with the explicit caveat that too few samples were tested to know how widespread it is. In the Mid-Atlantic it peaked at 46% of fentanyl samples in late 2024 and had fallen to 4% a year later.

checking.note: HAND-CURATED from live-verified sources. Every url returned HTTP 200 on lastVerified date via browser UA. This is the fastest-rotting data in the app - re-verify before trusting. Dead as of 2026-08-10 and deliberately EXCLUDED: testri.org (no connection), dancesafe.org/chapters (404), NASTAD participant pages (none exist).
checking.reality: Direct-to-individual lab checking is scarce but not zero. DrugsData paused intake in April 2024 under DEA order (no change expected before 2027); UNC's national mail-in program works through harm reduction organizations. Community-run services are emerging - Rebel Analytics in NYC advertises free testing with a mail-based expansion. For most people the practical route is still a local program: most US drug checking lives inside syringe service programs.

national.name: UNC Street Drug Analysis Lab
national.access: Ask a local syringe service program or harm reduction org to submit for you; the lab offers free kits to any US public health harm reduction organization. Free for NC organizations and drug user unions.
national.anon: The lab states it holds nothing about individuals: no names, nothing.

national.name: Rebel Analytics (Rebel Harm Reduction)
national.access: Free, community-funded testing (FTIR, immunoassay strips, reagents, lab-partner mass spec). Their site describes a mail option for people outside NYC but does not publish which states, turnaround, or intake rules - contact them before sending anything.
national.anon: Anonymity policy not published on their site - ask them directly.
national.caveat: Details verified only as far as their own pages state them, 2026-08-10.

national.name: DrugsData (Erowid)
national.access: Not accepting samples since April 2024 (DEA order); no change expected before 2027, per their homepage. The archive of past results remains searchable and useful.

national.name: NEXT Distro
national.access: Mail-based naloxone and fentanyl test strips - strips are self-testing, not lab checking. Availability varies by state law.

programs.name: MADDS / StreetCheck
programs.access: Free through partner orgs in ~19 communities; anonymous option. Accepts powders, rocks, pills, single-use pipes/cookers/cottons, baggies with residue. Not syringes or plant matter.

programs.name: NYC Health drug checking at SSPs
programs.access: Walk-in with a trained technician (FTIR + strips). Powders and pills; plant matter and most liquids cannot be tested. Call ahead to confirm.

NC Safer Syringe Initiative directory
programs.access: Drug checking reaches individuals through SSPs; the UNC lab is free in-state.

programs.name: Rapid Analysis of Drugs (RAD)
programs.access: Through Maryland SSPs only - residue swabs from used equipment, deidentified. Ask your SSP.

programs.name: Vermont community drug checking
programs.access: Legal statewide since 2023; availability varies by site - ask your syringe service program.

programs.name: WA Community Drug Checking Network
programs.access: Anonymous; drug or residue in a pipe or cooker. Not every site is listed - ask a local harm reduction agency.

programs.name: SCOPE - SF AIDS Foundation
programs.access: Free, anonymous, drop-in FTIR. 117 6th St (Mon 3-6, Tue-Wed 12-6) and 558 Clayton St (Fri 5:30-7:15). About 10-15 minutes; one sample per person per day. Call/text 415-361-8183.

programs.name: CDPH community drug checking
programs.access: Runs through partner orgs; no public site list exists. Free test strips at CDPH clinics, or email osu.cdph@cityofchicago.org.

orgs.scope: National buyers’ club supplying local programs
orgs.access: Open to any organization or program that gives harm reduction supplies away free. Not a direct supplier to individuals — it is how the program near you affords what it hands out, and where to start if you want to run one.

communities.headline: Finding your people
communities.intro: Most help is built around one kind of person: white, straight, housed, documented, insured. If that is not you, the hard part is often not finding help — it is explaining yourself before you can get any. These are places where the explaining is already done.
communities.howChecked: Every number and link here was opened and read on 2026-08-12, not copied from a directory. Anything we could not confirm was left out, and the gaps are named rather than filled.

keyNote.title: Some lines call the police. Some will not.
keyNote.body: A crisis line can send police or an ambulance to your address without asking you first. That is called active rescue, and for a lot of people it is the reason not to call at all. Where an organization publishes its policy, it is marked below in its own words. Where an organization does not publish one, it is left unmarked — that means unknown, not safe.
keyNote.detail: This matters more if you use drugs, are undocumented, are trans, are on parole, or have had police called on you before.

groups.title: LGBTQIA+ and trans people
groups.blurb: Two of these lines have a written policy against calling police on you. That is rare, and it is why they lead.

items.name: Trans Lifeline
items.what: Peer support staffed by trans people.
items.policyQuote: “We will not call emergency services or law enforcement without your explicit request — even if you tell us you or someone else is in danger.”
items.caution: Their microgrants program is paused, so do not count on it.

items.name: LGBT National Hotline
items.hours: Mon–Fri 2pm–11pm Eastern, Sat noon–5pm Eastern. Closed Sunday.
items.what: Peer support from LGBTQIA+ volunteers, any age.
items.policyQuote: “We don’t call other suicide hotlines, 911, or rescue services on your behalf.”

items.name: LGBT National Youth Talkline
items.what: The same service, for younger people.

items.name: LGBT National Senior Hotline
items.what: The same service, for older people.
items.caution: If you were given a SAGE elder hotline number, it stopped working in 2023 — many websites still list it. This is the working one.

items.name: The Trevor Project
items.what: Crisis support for LGBTQ+ people aged 13–24.
items.policyQuote: In their words, counselors “may need to contact a child welfare agency or emergency service” in some situations.

groups.gap: There is no national organization for trans people specifically around drug use or overdose. We looked hard. A UK-facing site with a similar name comes up in searches and does not serve the US.

groups.title: Black communities
groups.blurb: Mostly directories and funded therapy rather than crisis lines — so worth setting up before you need it, not during.

items.name: The Steve Fund
items.what: Mental health support for young people of color. The only round-the-clock option in this group.

items.name: BEAM (Black Emotional and Mental Health Collective)
items.what: A directory of Black therapists and wellness practitioners, plus free toolkits.
items.caution: No crisis line. In-person healing circles are in Los Angeles and Atlanta only; the directory is national.

items.name: Therapy for Black Girls
items.what: A searchable directory of therapists who work with Black women and girls.

items.name: The Loveland Foundation
items.what: Pays for 4–12 therapy sessions for Black women and nonbinary people.
items.caution: Applications open quarterly and replies take four to six weeks. Not a same-day resource.

items.name: Black Men Heal
items.what: Eight free virtual therapy sessions with providers of color.
items.caution: Only for residents of PA, NJ, DE, NYC, MD, DC, VA and GA, with a one-to-three-month waitlist.

items.name: Boris Lawrence Henson Foundation
items.what: Five free therapy sessions, open to anyone from age 12 regardless of insurance.
items.caution: Enrollment opens in rounds rather than continuously — check whether it is open.

groups.title: Native and Indigenous people
groups.blurb: Overdose death rates are higher here than in any other racial group in the US, and the national support to match does not exist yet. This is what we could actually verify.

items.name: White Bison / Wellbriety
items.what: Native-run recovery circles, online and in person, plus a directory of Wellbriety-certified treatment centers.
items.note: The strongest national Native-led option for substance use that we could confirm.

items.name: StrongHearts Native Helpline
items.what: Native advocates, for domestic and sexual violence.
items.caution: This is a domestic and sexual violence line — not a drug or overdose line.

items.name: We R Native
items.what: Health information by and for Native youth, including substance use and grief, with an anonymous ask-a-question service.

items.name: Urban Indian health clinic directory
items.what: Find a Native-serving clinic in or near your city.

groups.gap: There is no national Native-specific overdose or drug-use helpline. Several good programs exist but are local — Native and Strong (Washington State, dial 988 and press 4), NARA NW (Portland, Oregon), Indigenous Wellbriety (southwest Colorado). If one is near you it is worth more than anything national on this page.

items.name: SAMHSA National Helpline
items.what: Free and confidential. Referrals to local treatment, support groups and community programs.

items.name: Su Familia — National Hispanic Family Health Helpline
items.what: Bilingual health questions and referrals to care in your area.
items.caution: General health, not substance use specifically, and business hours only.

items.name: Latinx Therapy
items.what: A national directory for finding Latinx therapists.

groups.title: Survivors of abuse and violence
groups.blurb: If someone controls your access to drugs, or uses your using against you, that has a name and there are people who work on exactly it.

items.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline
items.what: Phone, text or chat.

items.name: National Sexual Assault Hotline (RAINN)
items.what: Anonymous unless you give your name and location.
items.policyQuote: In their words, if you share your name and location and are under 18 or a vulnerable adult, they are “required by law to report to authorities.” Staying anonymous keeps the session confidential.

items.name: The Deaf Hotline
items.what: ASL hotline for Deaf, DeafBlind and hard-of-hearing survivors.

items.name: National Center on Domestic Violence, Trauma and Mental Health
items.what: The national resource on substance use coercion — when the person harming you forces you to use, controls your supply, or blocks your access to recovery.
items.caution: Written material and referrals, not a crisis line.

groups.title: Sex workers
groups.blurb: Peer-run, by people who have done the work themselves.

items.name: SWOP Behind Bars — Community Support Line
items.hours: Hours are not published. Try it, but do not count on it being answered at 4am.
items.what: A national peer line answered by sex workers and survivors — safety planning, resources, and support after an arrest or an assault. Voice or chat. In their words: “All of our services and support are provided by other sex workers and survivors.”
items.caution: They publish nothing about whether they would ever contact police or emergency services, so treat that as unknown rather than as a no.

items.name: Lyon-Martin Community Health Services
items.hours: Harm reduction supplies drop-in Tuesdays 5–7pm, plus normal clinic hours.
items.what: San Francisco only. A clinic that took over St. James Infirmary's street outreach in 2024 and gives out harm reduction and safer sex supplies with no appointment. Primary care, gender-affirming care, and addiction medicine for trans, intersex and cisgender women, and for street-based sex workers.
items.caution: Local to San Francisco. Nothing national replaced St. James Infirmary's harm reduction program when it closed in December 2023 — that gap is real and we have not found anyone filling it.

items.name: SWOP Los Angeles
items.what: Monthly street outreach with condoms, lube, naloxone, water and cash, plus peer support twice a month. Email only, and they ask you not to DM them for your own safety.
items.caution: Los Angeles only.

items.name: SWOP Minneapolis
items.what: Harm reduction and naloxone, connected to the Minneapolis Stripper Guild. Email only, no phone.
items.caution: Minneapolis only.

groups.gap: SWOP USA's own site lists chapters in Hawaii, Philadelphia, Denton, Grand Rapids, Orlando, Houston and Austin. We checked every one: most of those domains no longer resolve, Houston's has not been touched since 2015, and SWOP USA publishes no working phone number and no working contact page. We are not linking chapters we could not confirm are still there — but it means this list is much shorter than the movement actually is. If you know a live local group, tell us.

groups.title: Pregnant or parenting
groups.blurb: The fear of losing a child is the single biggest reason people avoid help here. That fear is reasonable, and the answer depends heavily on your state — so the most useful thing we can give you is a free lawyer rather than our own guess.

items.name: Repro Legal Helpline
items.what: Free, confidential legal help about pregnancy, parenting and child protective services — in all 50 states, whatever your age or immigration status.
items.note: If you have one question about what could happen to you, ask it here.

items.name: Pregnancy Justice
items.what: Defends people facing criminal charges or child-welfare action over drug use during pregnancy.
items.caution: A legal organization, not a helpline. Replies are not immediate.

items.name: Academy of Perinatal Harm Reduction
items.what: Know-your-rights guides and birth planning for pregnant and parenting people who use drugs.

law.title: What the law actually says
law.body: Federal law requires hospitals to notify child welfare about a newborn affected by substance use, and to make a written “Plan of Safe Care.” Federal law also says that this notification is not by itself a finding of child abuse.
law.detail: What happens after that depends on your state, and states differ a great deal. We are not going to guess yours. The Repro Legal Helpline above is free and will tell you.

sources.name: Parental substance use as child maltreatment (Child Welfare Information Gateway)

groups.title: Deaf, hard of hearing, and disabled people

items.name: Deaf Crisis Line
items.what: Counselors fluent in ASL.

items.name: 988 by videophone, text or relay
items.what: Call 988 from a videophone number, text 988, chat online, or dial 711 then 988.

groups.gap: There is no national disability-specific substance use helpline. Mail-order naloxone is often the most practical route if getting somewhere is the barrier.

items.name: Veterans Crisis Line
items.what: You do not need to be enrolled in VA care.

groups.title: Leaving jail or prison
groups.blurb: This is the most dangerous window in the whole app. Tolerance drops fast inside, and the amount that was normal before is now enough to stop your breathing on the first day out — the risk of a fatal opioid overdose in the first two weeks after release has been measured at about 40 times the general population's — that is the first two weeks after release, from a North Carolina study following 229,274 people. Almost nothing is built for this moment, so most of what follows is a general line that will take your call rather than a reentry service, because reentry services with phone numbers largely do not exist.

items.name: Never Use Alone
items.what: You give an address, stay on the line while you use, and if you stop responding for more than 30 seconds they send EMS to that address as an unresponsive person.
items.note: If you use in the first days out, this is the single most useful number here. Lost tolerance means a dose that used to be normal for you can stop your breathing, and alone in a room there is no one to notice it happening.

items.name: SAMHSA National Helpline
items.hours: 24/7, English and Spanish. Or text your ZIP to 435748.
items.what: Free referrals to local treatment, including methadone and buprenorphine programs if you need to pick up where you left off inside.
items.note: In their own words: “We will not ask you for any personal information. We may ask for your zip code.” No insurance, no ID, no address to call.

items.name: NEXT Distro
items.what: Mails free naloxone to all 50 states, DC and Puerto Rico, postage included.
items.note: Order it to wherever you are going before your release date, or have someone meet you with it. Mail rarely lands on day one.

items.what: Dial 211 for referrals to local shelter, food, benefits and treatment.
items.caution: About 200 independent local agencies rather than one service, so hours and quality vary a lot by area. They refer you to shelters — they do not hold a bed for you. They publish no policy on whether they send police, so treat that as unknown.

items.name: Oxford House
items.what: A national network of self-run sober houses. Vacancies are listed at oxfordvacancies.com.
items.caution: Not an emergency bed. Current residents interview you, and living there means staying abstinent.

items.name: National Call Center for Homeless Veterans
items.what: Free and confidential, for veterans who are homeless or at risk — and for a family member or friend calling on their behalf.
items.note: The only 24/7 national housing line we could verify, and it is veterans only.

items.name: Legal Action Center
items.what: New York for most things — but they help people ANYWHERE in the country who are denied access to, or penalized for, taking addiction medication.
items.note: That nationwide part applies whether or not you have ever been locked up. If methadone or buprenorphine is being used against you, this is the number.
items.caution: Phone intake only, and they change their hours deliberately, so call to find out. They do not take general probation or parole condition cases.

items.name: Root & Rebound Reentry Legal Hotline
items.what: California reentry law — records, housing, licensing, parole conditions.
items.note: They accept collect calls from prison and jail, so this one can be used before you are out.
items.caution: California only, and they are mid-upgrade on their phone system — if it does not connect, they are asking people to email roadmap@rootandrebound.org.

items.name: Recidivism Reduction Hotline
items.what: Housing, work, healthcare and legal referrals across all 100 North Carolina counties, run by people who have been incarcerated themselves.
items.caution: North Carolina only. A nonprofit, not a state program.

items.name: Center for Employment Opportunities
items.what: Paid transitional work starting soon after release, in about 30 cities across 12 states.
items.caution: You apply at a local site, not through the head office.

items.name: The Fortune Society
items.hours: Walk in Mon–Thu 8am–7pm, Fri 8am–4pm — no appointment
items.what: Housing, health and job services under one roof in Queens, New York.
items.caution: New York City only, and you have to get there in person.

law.title: Before you count on naloxone at release — and a warning
law.body: Only about a quarter of US prisons hand out naloxone when you leave, so ask well before your date rather than assuming. California is the strongest: kits are offered to everyone leaving state prison unless they decline, with no ID or diagnosis needed. Washington and Maryland have programs with conditions attached — Washington requires a documented opioid use disorder, and Maryland's law covers sentenced people but not pretrial releases. Ask your counselor, and if the answer is no, order from NEXT Distro above.
law.detail: The warning: in several states, getting naloxone or staying on methadone or buprenorphine runs through your supervising officer, which turns asking for help into a disclosure. Washington distributes community kits through supervision officers. New York relays participation in medication treatment to parole. In Connecticut, being revived with naloxone inside triggers a drug test and can bring disciplinary action, reclassification, or a report recording your name and number. In Pennsylvania, an overdose reversal in community corrections is logged into a police information network under your parole number. None of that is a reason not to carry naloxone — it is a reason to know who finds out, so you are deciding with the facts.
law.checked: Checked 2026-08-12. State programs and policies change; treat this as a starting point for a question, not a settled answer.

sources.name: Ranapurwala et al., Am J Public Health 2018 (N=229,274)

groups.gap: There is no national reentry helpline, no national peer line staffed by people who have been inside, no national program handing out naloxone at release, no national emergency housing line unless you are a veteran, and no national reentry legal helpline. 988 lists twelve populations it has tailored support for and formerly incarcerated people are not one of them. If you are on supervision and required to abstain while still using, we could not find a single organization anywhere in the country offering guidance you can phone for. These are absences we verified, not things you failed to find.

items.name: Students for Sensible Drug Policy
items.what: Youth-led chapters that run overdose response training and give out free harm reduction supplies.
items.caution: Chapter-based, so coverage depends on whether there is one near you.

items.name: DanceSafe
items.what: Drug checking supplies, mail-in lab testing, and peer education for music and nightlife.
items.caution: Most supplies are bought, not free.

groups.title: If immigration status is part of the fear
groups.blurb: We are not going to tell you whether to call 911. We will tell you what we could and could not verify, and let you decide.

items.name: Never Use Alone
items.what: You give an address, stay on the line while you use, and if you stop responding for more than 30 seconds they send EMS to that address as an unresponsive person.
items.note: Worth knowing exactly what that means before you call: no one is dispatched because you called or because you said you use — only if you go quiet.

items.name: United We Dream — MigraWatch
items.what: Report ICE activity and get know-your-rights materials.
items.caution: Not an emergency line — it cannot send medical help. During an overdose, 911 or Never Use Alone (1-800-484-3731) can.

law.title: What we could verify about hospitals
law.body: The federal policy that used to limit immigration enforcement at hospitals and clinics was withdrawn in January 2025 and, as far as we could verify, has not been reinstated. Enforcement decisions are now made case by case.
law.detail: What appears to remain true: agents may enter public areas of a hospital, but non-public clinical areas require a valid judicial warrant or consent. Some states have passed their own protections and others have not. We are not able to tell you what applies where you are, and anyone who tells you confidently that hospitals are either safe or unsafe is overstating what is known.
law.checked: Checked 2026-08-12. This one changes — treat it as a starting point, not a settled answer.

groups.title: If you love someone who uses
groups.blurb: Groups that will not tell you to cut them off. Free, online, and they do not ask anyone to be abstinent.

items.name: Friends & Family — Harm Reduction Works
items.what: A peer-run meeting built by people who use drugs, as a deliberate alternative to the abstinence-only groups. Free, online, and you can dial in by phone instead of using the app. There is a Parents and Guardians meeting on Mondays at 7pm Eastern.
items.caution: Open the calendar rather than saving a meeting link — the links change.

items.name: Invitation to Change — CMC:Foundation for Change
items.hours: Several weekly groups, including a national one Tuesdays 12pm Eastern.
items.what: Free peer-led groups for anyone helping someone who uses. Built around staying connected to the person rather than issuing ultimatums. Their own framing is that Al-Anon is often the only thing offered and does not teach evidence-based strategies.
items.caution: The group finder sometimes hangs on “Loading” and drops you to a newsletter box — that does not mean nothing is running. Separate paid “Family Mondays” sessions cost $15; the groups themselves are free.

items.name: Partnership to End Addiction helpline
items.what: Free coaching for families. Harm reduction inclusive in their own words — they will talk about using more safely or cutting back, not only about stopping.
items.caution: In their own words they are not affiliated with any treatment provider and will not refer to programs they have not vetted — which is worth knowing, because most “helplines” you find by searching are paid referral services.

groups.gap: No organization in the US runs a staffed phone line for families wanting harm reduction guidance. The two groups above meet on a schedule; there is nothing for a parent awake at 2am. We looked hard for one.

groups.title: If someone died
groups.blurb: Overdose grief is its own thing. People bring casseroles when someone dies of anything else.

items.name: GRASP — Grief Recovery After a Substance Passing
items.what: Free peer support meetings for people who lost someone to overdose or substance use.
items.caution: An office line, not a crisis line. Meetings are local, so availability varies.

items.name: Team Sharing
items.what: A national network of parents who lost a child to substance use.

communities.closing: If nothing here fits, that is a real answer and not your failure. Several of these gaps are things that do not exist yet in the United States, not things you failed to find.

conditions.note: Session-only condition lens. Selections are NEVER stored - see the module comment in substances.js. Each caution's source was live-verified 2026-08-10, except the gender-affirming hormone entries, verified 2026-08-14. Conditions appear only when the reader picks them.

conditions.label: Heart condition or high blood pressure

items.text: Methadone carries a boxed warning for life-threatening heart rhythm changes (QT prolongation). Other QT-prolonging drugs add to it.
Stimulants raise heart rate and blood pressure while they act - that is their mechanism, not a side effect. A heart condition changes what a normal-for-others amount does to you.

sources.name: See stimulant class pages and their cited labels

items.text: Tramadol lowers the seizure threshold - its label carries a dedicated seizure warning - and the risk rises further combined with SSRIs or SNRIs.
Stopping benzodiazepines abruptly after regular use can itself cause seizures - one of the few cases where quitting suddenly is more dangerous than tapering.
SSRI and SNRI labels list amphetamines (including MDMA) among serotonin-syndrome risks. MAOIs are the serious one: contraindicated with serotonergic drugs, with documented severe reactions.
SSRIs also blunt most of MDMA's effect - which people sometimes answer by taking more. The blunting is documented; taking more is the danger.

conditions.label: On HIV treatment with a booster

items.text: Ritonavir and cobicistat block the enzyme that clears fentanyl, several benzos, and others - raising their levels. Documented deaths exist with MDMA. Check your exact pair on the Liverpool checker; PrEP alone is not a booster.

Each has its own section under "On prescribed medication?" below - naltrexone especially: tolerance drops during treatment, and opioid use after a missed dose carries heightened overdose risk per its label.

Spironolactone moves your electrolytes in two directions at once. Its label warns that excessive diuresis may cause symptomatic dehydration, and that it can cause hyponatremia — low sodium. The dancefloor advice everywhere, including on this site, about drinking water in heat is written for people whose sodium starts normal. It also causes hyperkalemia, high potassium, which is the label's lead warning and a contraindication — and stimulant overheating releases potassium from muscle.

Estrogen raises the risk of a blood clot, and this is the risk that has actually been measured in trans people rather than borrowed from somebody else. Across 18 studies covering 11,542 people on feminizing hormones, about 2 in 100 had a clot. It concentrates in one form: ethinylestradiol, the estrogen in older birth-control pills and in a lot of what is sold without a prescription, ran 2 to 6 in 100 — roughly twenty times the rate in cis men. Estradiol through the skin does not show the same rise, because swallowing it sends it through the liver first and that is where the clotting factors go up. Long hours sitting still, dehydration and smoking stack on top.

sources.name: Pooled VTE prevalence, 18 studies, 11,542 people (Front Endocrinol 2021)
VTE in transgender women — route of administration (2023 review)

items.text: Testosterone thickens your blood — it raises hematocrit, which is why prescribers check bloodwork. Be clear about what that does and does not mean: the clot warnings printed on testosterone labels come from replacement therapy in cis men, and the studies that have looked at trans men specifically have not found an increased clot risk. The label's own instruction if hematocrit runs high is to stop until it comes down, not to keep going — so this is a reason to get the blood test, not a reason to stop on your own.

sources.name: Managing VTE risk in transgender adults on hormone therapy

items.text: Testosterone is a Schedule III controlled substance. Holding it without a prescription is a drug charge, and that matters most if you are on probation or parole — the same exposure as anything else in your pocket. Not a reason not to have it. A reason to know who finds out.

sources.name: What supervision can and cannot require

items.text: If you are on HIV treatment as well, boosters and inducers move hormone levels in both directions — some push estradiol up, others cut it by a third. Liverpool keeps a chart for exactly this pairing.

sources.name: Liverpool — gender-affirming therapy × HIV drug interactions (Nov 2025)

conditions.notCovered: Pregnancy, liver and kidney disease, diabetes, asthma, and mental health conditions are real factors we have not yet sourced to this app's standard. Nor is whether estrogen changes how a stimulant hits you — that has been studied in rats and not in people — or whether kratom raises estradiol levels, which nobody has tested. Their absence here is a gap in this page, never evidence of safety.

consent.headline: Consent and making things right
consent.blurb: Two things almost nobody is taught: how to be sure someone actually wants what is happening when substances are involved, and what to do once you have hurt somebody and want to fix it.

consent.title: Consent when people are high
consent.intro: Most people who use drugs never hurt anyone. This is here because the rules everyone learned were written for sober rooms, and nobody hands you a new set at the door.

callout.title: If you are asking yourself whether they are too out of it, that is your answer
callout.body: You do not have to work out where the line is. The fact that you are wondering means you are near it, and a good night is nowhere near that line.
callout.detail: Wait. If they want you in the morning, they will still want you in the morning.

items.t: There is no amount that makes it fine
items.b: No number of drinks, no dose, no half hour of waiting. People have different tolerances and different bodies, and the same amount lands differently on the same person on a different night. There is no line to measure.

items.t: Asking how high they are does not settle it
items.b: Someone who is very high often cannot tell you how high they are — that is part of being high. Their answer is not a green light. Ask anyway if you like, but do not treat it as proof.

items.t: Being high yourself does not hand the job to anyone else
items.b: If you are the one starting something, checking is yours to do. Nobody is going to accept that you were too far gone to notice, and more importantly, the person you hurt will not get that time back.

items.t: A yes while high is not always the yes they would have given
items.b: People agree to things on drugs that they would not have agreed to sober, and wake up feeling like something was taken. If you never talked about this while everyone was sober, waiting is the move.

items.t: Being near you is not permission
items.b: Dancing close, smiling, ending up in the same pile of people at 5am — none of that is a yes to being touched. Ask first. Every time, and about each new thing.

items.t: You are not owed anything for kindness
items.b: Buying someone drinks, sharing what you have, sitting with them while they come down, walking them home — those are good things to do and they buy you nothing. Using them as leverage turns a kindness into a debt collection.

items.t: Never give someone a drug they are not expecting
items.b: Not as a joke, not as a gift, not because you think they would love it. Being dosed without knowing is frightening in a way that lasts, and it takes away the one thing a person has here: the choice about what goes in their body.

items.t: Pushing more into someone is its own harm
items.b: Pressuring somebody past what they wanted, or not telling them what is actually in what they are taking, is on the list of ways people get hurt — not a gray area. So is walking away from someone having a bad time who asked for help.

items.t: Arousal is not consent
items.b: Getting hard, getting wet, or coming are involuntary. The body does them without agreement and sometimes during an assault. None of them means yes, and none of them cancels a no. This matters more when someone is high, because a body on drugs is doing all sorts of things the person did not ask it to.

items.t: Going still is a no
items.b: People freeze. They go quiet, stop moving, turn their face away, or seem to check out. That is not consent arriving — it is often consent leaving, and it is one of the most common ways a body responds to fear. If someone goes still or silent, stop and ask. Do not read stillness as permission.

items.t: Once you know they are not into it, stop asking
items.b: Asking again after a no is pressure, even when it is polite, even when you are gentle about it. Wearing someone down until they stop saying no is not the same as them saying yes.

items.t: Agree on a signal before anyone is high
items.b: Speech is the first thing to go. Pick something physical that works when words do not — squeezing a leg twice, stomping, dropping something, shaking your head. Agree on it while everyone is still clear, and agree that it stops everything, no discussion. This is standard practice in kink communities and it transfers directly to being high.

items.t: Men get assaulted, and it is mostly not talked about
items.b: In a CDC survey of 6,767 US men, 16.9% reported contact sexual violence at some point in their lives, and 3.8% reported being made to penetrate someone else — which is more than the 3.2% who reported rape, and which US surveys do not count as rape. In earlier CDC data, most men who were made to penetrate reported only female perpetrators. If this happened to you, it happened. The lines below are for you too.

items.t: Whether being high cancels consent is state law, not one rule
items.b: Every state treats intoxication and the ability to consent differently, and some carve out voluntary intoxication specifically. That is a legal question with a different answer depending on where you are standing. It does not change the practical one: if you cannot tell whether someone is able to agree, you do not have agreement.

after.title: If you think somebody was drugged
body: It is far more common for someone to take advantage of drugs a person already took than for a stranger to spike a drink — and alcohol is the substance involved most often. Either way, none of it is the fault of the person it happened to.

Urine can be worth collecting up to 96 hours after — that is the window the US Department of Justice tells examiners to work to, and it is longer than most sources say. Sooner is much better, and the first time you pee is the best sample. If you cannot get to a hospital right away, pee into a clean container with a lid and put it in the fridge or freezer. It keeps the option open. Tell the staff you think there was drugging, so they run the right tests. Blood is a shorter window, about 24 hours.
The National Sexual Assault Hotline is 800-656-4673, 24 hours. It is anonymous unless you give your name and location.
