repair.title: After you have hurt someone
repair.intro: Crossing a line does not make you a bad person — what you do next is the part that is actually yours. This is not about groveling, and it is not about being forgiven. Neither of those helps the person you hurt.

framework.title: The four parts, if you want a map
framework.credit: The structure underneath all of this is Mia Mingus's, from her essay “The Four Parts of Accountability” (2019). She wrote it for conflict, hurt feelings and small breaks in trust — not for serious harm, violence or abuse. If what happened was serious, this is not enough on its own, and it is worth finding someone experienced to help.

parts.name: Work out what you did
parts.what: Before anything else, you have to actually see it — not the version where you were misunderstood. That is the part nobody can do for you, and everything after it is hollow without it.

parts.name: Apologize
parts.what: Say the words, name the specific thing you did, and name what it did to them. Not what you meant. What happened.

parts.name: Repair
parts.what: Do something about it, and rebuild trust so they can believe it will not happen again. This part is slow and it does not go in a straight line.

parts.name: Change what you do
parts.what: The hardest one. If you apologize and make it right again and again but keep doing the same thing, people stop believing you — and they are right to.

apology.title: What an apology needs, and what wrecks one
helps: Actually say “I'm sorry.” A surprising number of apologies never include it.
Name the thing plainly. If you crossed a line, say you crossed a line — not that things “got confusing.”
Say what it did to them, not what you meant by it.
Say what you will do differently, then do it.
Ask what would help, instead of deciding what would help.
hurts: Apologizing so that they will comfort you, or so they will apologize back. That is not an apology, it is a trade.
Falling apart so hard that they end up looking after you. Your feelings are real and they are not their job right now.
Rushing to smooth it over or explain what you meant — it lands as being told it did not happen.
Treating forgiveness as the finish line. You are not owed it, and not getting it does not make you a monster.
Apologizing when you do not mean it. A hollow apology does more damage than saying nothing.

caution.title: Sometimes the apology is for you, not for them
caution.body: Turning up to make amends can land on somebody as one more thing being done to them — especially if they have been trying not to think about it, or if seeing you is frightening. Even AA's ninth step, which is all about making amends directly, stops at “except when to do so would injure them or others.”
caution.detail: So check before you go: is this to put something right, or to feel better? Would it cost them anything to receive it? If you are not sure, ask someone else first, or write it and do not send it. Nobody is ever obliged to accept an apology, and someone deciding they do not want contact is an answer, not a door left open.

shame.title: Feeling terrible is not the same as fixing it
body: There is a difference between “I did something bad” and “I am bad.” The research on this is fairly consistent: the first tends to lead people to own up, apologize and put things right, and the second tends to lead to hiding, getting defensive, and lashing out. Shame does not make people behave better — it mostly makes them harder to reach.

That matters more here than most places. Feeling like a bad person is tangled up with using more, and drowning in it is not accountability. It looks like it from the inside, because it hurts, but the person you hurt gets nothing out of your suffering.

One honest caveat: most of this research was done on college students, and one study of people with substance problems could not find the same clean split between the two feelings. So treat it as a useful way to steer yourself, not as a law.

When “I am a bad person” shows up, answer it directly: I do not want to be someone who does that, and I am going to fix what I can. That is not letting yourself off — it is the difference between a person who changes and a person who hides.

sources.name: Mia Mingus — the four parts of accountability
Tangney et al., Annual Review of Psychology (2007)
National Domestic Violence Hotline — if an abusive partner apologizes

first.title: The first five minutes
first.body: Your feelings are real and they are not the focus right now. The instinct is to explain what you meant, or to fall apart — both land on the other person as being told it did not happen, or as a job to manage you.
scripts: “Can you help me understand what just happened? I don't want this to happen again.”
first.note: Then stop talking and listen to the answer, including if the answer is that they want you to go away.

descriptions.note: HAND-WRITTEN plain-language descriptions, for a reader who has never encountered a substance and does not know what it is. PsychonautWiki cannot supply these: its `summary` field is a scraped warning box that is frequently junk ("Summary sheet: MDMA MDMA"), and its `effects` field returns only the substance's own name. Both were checked against the live API on 2026-08-10 before writing these by hand. A second batch was written on 2026-08-15 for substances whose ordinary identity IS the description - a supplement, a spice, an over-the-counter box, a prescription somebody already holds. Those did not need a published effects write-up to be describable, and leaving them blank was the wrong call: a reader who does not know that myristicin is nutmeg cannot assess anything else on the page. Where the effects genuinely are not documented, the description says so rather than inventing them.
rules: Say what it IS and what people take it FOR. Someone who does not know cannot assess a warning about it.
No dosing, no route advice, no how-to. Dose ranges already live in their own section with their own caveats.
Neither advertise nor frighten. 'Euphoric' oversells; 'deadly poison' is the fear-based framing EVIDENCE.md rejects. Describe.
Name the ordinary medical use where there is one - most people meet oxycodone, ketamine and diazepam in a hospital first.
Plain words. Roughly an 8th-grade reading level, no pharmacology unless it changes what someone would do.
Where the thing has an ordinary identity - a supplement, a spice, an OTC box, a prescription - lead with that. What it says on the packaging is a checkable fact and it is what the reader recognizes.
Where nobody has published what it DOES, say so plainly and still say what it IS. An absence of effects data is not an absence of identity.

descriptions.alcohol: The drug in beer, wine and spirits. It slows the brain and body down, which is why it makes people relaxed and unsteady — and why it gets dangerous next to other things that slow you down, like opioids or benzos. It is legal and completely ordinary, and that is exactly why people forget it belongs on this list.
descriptions.cannabis: The dried flower of the cannabis plant, smoked, vaped or eaten. What it does varies a lot between people and between strains — usually relaxation, changed senses and hunger, though some people get anxiety or a racing heart instead. Eaten, it takes much longer to come on than smoked, and that is the single most common way people take more than they meant to.
descriptions.mdma: A stimulant that also does something to your feelings, sold as ecstasy or molly, in pills or powder. People take it for warmth, closeness and energy, mostly around other people and music. It pushes up your body temperature and heart rate. A lot of what gets sold under these names is not MDMA at all.
descriptions.lsd: A psychedelic, usually sold on small squares of blotter paper. It changes how you see, think and feel for a long time — eight to twelve hours is normal, which is far longer than most people expect the first time. The risk is not your breathing — it is that long stretch of altered judgement, and how badly a difficult one can go. That depends a lot on your mood, who you are with and where you are.
descriptions.psilocybin-mushrooms: Mushrooms containing psilocybin, sometimes called magic mushrooms or shrooms, usually eaten dried or brewed into tea. You get visual changes, shifts in thinking and mood, and often strong emotion, for about four to six hours. The main physical danger is picking the wrong wild mushroom, not the psilocybin.
descriptions.ketamine: An anesthetic used in hospitals and by vets, also used as a powder to get high. It makes you feel detached from your body and your surroundings, and at higher amounts you can end up unable to move or respond at all — which is dangerous around vomiting, water, or being on your own. Using a lot, regularly, is strongly linked to serious bladder damage.
descriptions.cocaine: A stimulant made from the coca plant, sold as a white powder. It makes you alert, confident and full of energy for a short time — often under an hour — which is why people keep going back for more. It puts strain on the heart, and mixing it with alcohol makes your body create a third substance that is harder on the heart than either one alone.
descriptions.crack-cocaine: Cocaine cooked into a smokable rock. Same drug as powder, but smoking gets it there faster and it wears off sooner, so people redose more often and dependence builds more easily.
descriptions.heroin: An opioid made from morphine, sold as powder or sticky tar. It kills pain and brings warmth and heavy sedation. Across much of the US, what is sold as heroin now has fentanyl in it, or simply is fentanyl — which is why strength can change without warning from one batch to the next.
descriptions.fentanyl: A synthetic opioid used in hospitals for severe pain, and now the main opioid in the street supply. It works in far smaller amounts than heroin, so it is very hard to mix evenly — two scoops out of the same bag can be different strengths. It also turns up in drugs nobody sold as opioids at all.
descriptions.methamphetamine: A stimulant that lasts a long time, sold as crystals or powder. It keeps you alert, energetic and awake for many hours — much longer than cocaine. Using a lot of it, or using for a long time, is linked to losing sleep and weight, damage to your teeth, and paranoia or psychosis that can hang around after you stop.
descriptions.amphetamine: A stimulant, prescribed as Adderall for ADHD and also used without a prescription. It sharpens focus, gives you energy, keeps you awake and kills appetite. The prescribed and street versions are the same drug — the difference is that a prescription comes with a known strength.
descriptions.methylphenidate: A stimulant prescribed as Ritalin or Concerta, mostly for ADHD. It sharpens focus and gives you energy, and does not last as long as amphetamine.
descriptions.alprazolam: A benzodiazepine, prescribed as Xanax for anxiety and panic. It calms you, sedates you, and wipes your memory of the hours you were on it. Mixed with opioids or alcohol it is one of the most common things found in fatal overdoses, and pressed pills sold as Xanax very often contain something else entirely.
descriptions.diazepam: A benzodiazepine, prescribed as Valium for anxiety, muscle spasm and alcohol withdrawal. It lasts longer than most of its family. Stopping suddenly after using it regularly can cause seizures — it is one of the few drugs where quitting cold turkey is more dangerous than coming off slowly.
descriptions.oxycodone: An opioid painkiller, prescribed as OxyContin or Percocet. It kills pain, sedates you and brings euphoria. Pills sold as oxycodone outside a pharmacy — especially ones stamped M30 — are very often pressed fentanyl instead.
descriptions.codeine: A weaker opioid, in some prescription cough syrups and pain tablets. Your body turns it into morphine, and how much it turns varies a lot person to person — so the same tablet hits two people differently.
descriptions.buprenorphine: An opioid used to treat opioid dependence and pain, prescribed as Suboxone or Subutex. It sits on the same receptors without doing the same thing, which takes away withdrawal and cravings. Because it grips those receptors so tightly, taking it too soon after another opioid can throw you straight into withdrawal.
descriptions.tramadol: A prescription painkiller that works partly like a weak opioid and also messes with serotonin. That second part is why it reacts badly with antidepressants and raises the chance of a seizure — it does not behave like other opioids of similar strength.
descriptions.kratom: The leaf of a Southeast Asian tree, taken as powder, capsules or tea. Smaller amounts feel more like a stimulant, larger amounts more like a mild opioid. Some people use it for pain, or to get through opioid withdrawal. Using it regularly can build dependence, with a withdrawal of its own.
descriptions.ghb: A depressant sold as a salty liquid, used to get high and sometimes to sleep. Here is the thing that makes it dangerous: the amount that gets you high and the amount that knocks you out are very close together. Drink alcohol with it and that gap gets smaller still.
descriptions.dmt: A very short, very intense psychedelic, usually smoked or vaped. It arrives within seconds and is usually over in fifteen to thirty minutes. It is also what makes ayahuasca work — combined with an MAOI it lasts hours instead, and that combination reacts seriously with a lot of medications.
descriptions.mescaline: A psychedelic found in peyote, San Pedro and related cacti, used in Indigenous ceremony for a very long time. Visual and emotional changes lasting roughly ten to twelve hours. Peyote grows slowly and is under threat, and its ceremonial use is legally protected for members of the Native American Church.
descriptions.2c-b: A synthetic psychedelic with a stimulant edge, sold as pills or powder. Shorter than LSD — usually four to eight hours. It belongs to a family of near-identical chemicals with very different strengths, and mixing one up for another is the usual way people get hurt with it.
descriptions.nitrous: Nitrous oxide, or laughing gas, used by dentists and to charge whipped cream canisters. Breathed in, you get about a minute of dizziness and distortion. Two specific dangers: suffocating if you breathe it without oxygen, and nerve damage from using a lot of it, because it strips out your vitamin B12.
descriptions.pregabalin: A prescription medicine for nerve pain, seizures and anxiety, sold as Lyrica. It is a depressant and piles onto the sedation from opioids and alcohol, which is why it shows up in overdose reports far more often than its reputation would suggest.
descriptions.gabapentin: A prescription medicine for nerve pain and seizures, sold as Neurontin. Like pregabalin it sedates you and stacks with opioids and alcohol. People tend to assume it is harmless because it is everywhere and handed out freely.
descriptions.methadone: An opioid that lasts a long time, used both to treat opioid dependence and for pain. It outlasts heroin or fentanyl by a long way — often more than a day — which is what makes it good for holding off withdrawal, and also what makes it dangerous: it stacks up in your body over the first few days of taking it.
descriptions.morphine: The original opioid painkiller, made from the opium poppy and still used in hospitals for severe pain. Nearly every other opioid gets measured against it.
descriptions.hydrocodone: An opioid painkiller, prescribed as Vicodin or Norco, usually mixed with acetaminophen. That mix matters: taking extra tablets to get more opioid also means more acetaminophen, and acetaminophen wrecks your liver.
descriptions.hydromorphone: A strong opioid painkiller, prescribed as Dilaudid, used in hospitals for severe pain. A good deal stronger than morphine, milligram for milligram.
descriptions.oxymorphone: A strong opioid painkiller, prescribed as Opana. Stronger than oxycodone, milligram for milligram.
descriptions.tapentadol: A prescription painkiller that works as an opioid and also acts on norepinephrine. Like tramadol, that second action means it reacts with antidepressants in ways other opioids do not.
descriptions.pethidine: An older opioid painkiller, also called meperidine or Demerol, once common in childbirth and surgery. Used far less now, because something it breaks down into builds up with repeated doses and can cause seizures.
descriptions.dihydrocodeine: An opioid painkiller about as strong as codeine, found in some prescription tablets and cough medicines.
descriptions.o-desmethyltramadol: What your body turns tramadol into — and the part that actually kills the pain. It also gets sold on its own, sometimes in things marketed as herbal, which is a problem: you have no idea of the strength and it carries tramadol's seizure risk.
descriptions.dextropropoxyphene: An opioid painkiller pulled from the US and much of Europe because it caused heart rhythm problems and deaths at amounts not far above a normal dose.
descriptions.acetylfentanyl: A fentanyl analogue — a chemical cousin of fentanyl. It was never made as a medicine and turns up in the street opioid supply. Like fentanyl, it works in tiny amounts, so it is hard to mix evenly.
descriptions.sufentanil: A hospital opioid, used in surgery and epidurals. Far stronger than fentanyl for the same amount, with no safe margin outside a clinical setting.
descriptions.u-47700: A synthetic opioid, sometimes sold as pink or U4. It was made for research, never approved as a medicine, and shows up in the street supply as a powder or pressed into counterfeit pills.
descriptions.dextromethorphan: The cough suppressant in a lot of over-the-counter cold medicines, often labeled DXM. In larger amounts it works as a dissociative, leaving you detached and altering what you perceive. The real practical danger is cold medicines that also contain acetaminophen or antihistamines, which turn toxic long before the DXM wears off.
descriptions.pcp: A dissociative anesthetic, also called angel dust, dropped from medical use because of how confused and agitated people were as it wore off. It leaves you detached from your body and your surroundings, and does unpredictable things to mood and behavior.
descriptions.mephedrone: A stimulant, also called 4-MMC or meow meow, sold as powder or in capsules. Energy and sociability for a short time, which is exactly why people redose.
descriptions.3-mmc: A stimulant closely related to mephedrone, sold after mephedrone got banned in a lot of countries. Similar effects, similarly short.
descriptions.a-pvp: A stimulant that lasts a long time, sometimes called flakka, part of the cathinone family. Effects can run for many hours, and at higher amounts it brings agitation, sleeplessness and confusion.
descriptions.methylone: A stimulant with a mild emotional edge, chemically related to MDMA but much weaker on that front. It has been sold as MDMA, and mixed into things labeled MDMA.
descriptions.mda: A psychedelic stimulant closely related to MDMA, sometimes called sally. Lasts longer than MDMA, with more visual effect and less of the emotional warmth.
descriptions.mdea: A drug closely related to MDMA, sometimes called eve, with a milder emotional effect.
descriptions.gbl: A liquid solvent that your body turns into GHB, with the same effects and the same tiny gap between the amount that gets you high and the amount that knocks you out. It hits faster than GHB, which makes that gap even harder to judge.
descriptions.baclofen: A prescription muscle relaxant for spasticity, sometimes used for alcohol dependence. It is a depressant and adds to what opioids and alcohol are already doing. Stopping it suddenly after regular use can cause serious withdrawal.
descriptions.mdai: A drug related to MDMA that brings emotional warmth without much stimulation. Sometimes sold as a legal stand-in for MDMA.
descriptions.5-apb: A stimulant with a psychedelic edge, sold as an MDMA substitute, and often lasting a lot longer than people expect.
descriptions.6-apb: A stimulant with a psychedelic edge, sometimes called benzo fury, sold as an MDMA substitute. It comes on slowly — the usual way people end up taking more than they meant to — and then lasts a long time.
descriptions.caffeine: The stimulant in coffee, tea and energy drinks, and a very common cutting agent in powders sold as something else. On its own it is mild; mixed into a stimulant it makes a bag look bigger without making it stronger.
descriptions.nicotine: The drug in tobacco and vapes. It is a stimulant, it builds dependence fast, and concentrated vape liquid is genuinely dangerous to swallow — especially around children.
descriptions.clonazepam: A benzodiazepine, prescribed as Klonopin for seizures and panic. Long-acting. Like the rest of its family it stacks with opioids and alcohol, and stopping suddenly after regular use can cause seizures.
descriptions.lorazepam: A benzodiazepine, prescribed as Ativan for anxiety and seizures. Shorter-acting than diazepam. Same two rules as the rest of the family: it stacks dangerously with opioids and alcohol, and coming off it needs to be gradual.
descriptions.zolpidem: A sleeping pill, prescribed as Ambien. Not a benzodiazepine but it acts on the same system and carries the same danger next to opioids and alcohol. It is well known for people doing things while apparently awake and having no memory of it.
descriptions.zopiclone: A sleeping pill, sold as Imovane or Zimovane. Like zolpidem it is not a benzodiazepine but behaves like one, including how badly it mixes with opioids and alcohol. Often leaves a metallic taste.
descriptions.eszopiclone: A sleeping pill, prescribed as Lunesta. Closely related to zopiclone and carries the same warning about mixing with opioids or alcohol.
descriptions.etizolam: A benzodiazepine-type drug prescribed in a few countries and sold widely online everywhere else. It is often what is actually in a pill sold as Xanax. Strength varies enormously batch to batch, which is what makes it dangerous alongside opioids.
descriptions.flualprazolam: A designer benzodiazepine, never a medicine anywhere. It turns up pressed into counterfeit Xanax and is considerably stronger than alprazolam, so a pill that looks familiar can be far more sedating than expected.
descriptions.flubromazolam: A designer benzodiazepine, never approved as a medicine. Very strong in very small amounts and long-lasting, which is a bad combination when nobody knows how much is in a pill.
descriptions.metizolam: A designer benzodiazepine sold online, never a medicine. Like the others in this group, the real problem is that the amount in any given pill is unknown.
descriptions.deschloroetizolam: A designer benzodiazepine related to etizolam, never approved as a medicine and not made to any consistent strength.
descriptions.phenibut: A Russian anxiety medicine sold as a supplement in the US. It is a depressant and adds to alcohol and opioids. Dependence builds faster than people expect, and the withdrawal is genuinely severe — closer to benzodiazepine withdrawal than to a hangover.
descriptions.f-phenibut: A stronger, faster version of phenibut, sold as a supplement. Same dependence and same severe withdrawal, reached sooner.
descriptions.modafinil: A prescription wakefulness drug, sold as Provigil, used for narcolepsy and shift work. It keeps you awake without much of a stimulant rush. It speeds up how the liver clears some medicines, which matters most for hormonal birth control.
descriptions.armodafinil: A longer-lasting version of modafinil, prescribed as Nuvigil, with the same effects and the same interaction with hormonal birth control.
descriptions.psilocin: What your body turns psilocybin into, and the part that actually does something. It is also what is measured when mushrooms are tested.
descriptions.datura: A plant — jimsonweed or thornapple — containing deliriants. This is not a psychedelic: people experience convincing hallucinations they cannot tell from real, often with no memory afterwards. The amount varies wildly between plants and even between parts of the same plant, and the gap between an active and a poisonous dose is small.
descriptions.ayahuasca: A brew from South America combining a DMT-containing plant with an MAOI plant, traditionally used in ceremony. The MAOI is what makes it last hours rather than minutes, and it is also the part that reacts dangerously with many antidepressants and with some foods.
descriptions.changa: DMT absorbed onto an herb blend that includes an MAOI, made to be smoked. It lasts longer than smoked DMT alone, and the MAOI brings the same medication interactions ayahuasca has.
descriptions.melatonin: A hormone your brain makes at night to time your sleep. The version sold in shops is a supplement, taken to fall asleep or reset after a time-zone change. It is not a sedative and does not knock you out — it shifts when you feel sleepy rather than forcing it. It is on this list because it is a real drug people combine with others, not because it is dangerous on its own.
descriptions.myristicin: The active compound in nutmeg, the ordinary baking spice. In cooking amounts it does nothing but flavor food. People occasionally swallow large amounts of the spice for effect, which is well documented as an unpleasant experience — hours of nausea, a racing heart, dry mouth and confusion, coming on slowly and lasting a day or more.
descriptions.diphenhydramine: The antihistamine in Benadryl and in most "nighttime" or "PM" versions of painkillers. It is sold for allergies and to help people sleep. It is on this list for two reasons: at high amounts it causes confusion and hallucinations that people find genuinely frightening, and it adds to the sedation of anything else that slows you down.
descriptions.cannabidiol: CBD — a compound from the cannabis plant sold in oils, drinks and gummies. It does not get you high the way THC does. It is marketed for anxiety, pain and sleep; the evidence for that is thin outside of two rare seizure disorders, where a prescription version is genuinely effective. Products vary wildly in what they actually contain.
descriptions.kava: A drink made from the root of a Pacific Islands plant, traditional across Fiji, Vanuatu, Tonga and Samoa, and sold in the US in kava bars and as capsules. It relaxes people and numbs the mouth. Heavy long-term use has been linked to liver problems, and it adds to alcohol and other things that slow you down.
descriptions.blue-lotus: A water lily sold as dried flowers, tea, vapes and gummies, often marketed as a legal relaxant. It has a long history in ancient Egyptian art and a very short one in published research: almost nothing about its effects has been properly studied, so what it actually does at the amounts people take is not established. Products sold under the name vary in what is in them.
descriptions.creatine: A sports supplement, one of the most studied there is. It helps muscles produce short bursts of power, so people take it for strength training. It is not psychoactive — it is here because it turns up in stacks alongside things that are.
descriptions.theanine: An amino acid found in tea leaves, sold as a supplement and often paired with caffeine. People take it to take the edge off caffeine's jitteriness. Effects are mild; it is here because it is a common ingredient in energy and "focus" products.
descriptions.theacrine: A compound related to caffeine, found in kucha tea and sold in energy and pre-workout products. It is stimulating and appears to build less tolerance than caffeine. Human research on it is limited.
descriptions.alpha-gpc: A choline supplement sold for memory and focus, and used in some countries as a prescription drug after a stroke. It is a building block your body uses to make a brain chemical involved in attention. Sold over the counter in the US as a nootropic.
descriptions.choline-bitartrate: A cheap, common form of choline, an essential nutrient found in eggs and liver. Sold as a supplement for memory and often taken alongside nootropics. Little of it reaches the brain compared with the other forms sold for the same purpose.
descriptions.citicoline: A choline supplement sold for memory and attention, and used as a prescription medicine in parts of Europe and Asia after strokes and head injuries. Sold over the counter in the US.
descriptions.n-acetylcysteine: NAC — a supplement, and also a hospital medicine: it is the antidote for acetaminophen (Tylenol) overdose, where it is genuinely life-saving. Over the counter it is sold for the lungs, the liver and, on thinner evidence, for cutting cravings.
descriptions.sam-e: A supplement sold for mood and joints, and a prescription drug for depression in several European countries. It is a substance your body already makes. It should not be combined with antidepressants without a doctor — that combination is a serotonin risk.
descriptions.tyrosine: An amino acid from ordinary protein in food, sold as a supplement. Your body uses it to build dopamine and adrenaline, which is why it is marketed for focus and for performing under stress. Effects in well-rested people are small.
descriptions.5-hydroxytryptophan: 5-HTP — a supplement your body converts into serotonin, sold for mood and sleep. Because it raises serotonin directly, it is a real interaction risk with antidepressants, MAOIs and MDMA rather than a harmless vitamin.
descriptions.galantamine: A prescription medicine for Alzheimer's disease, derived from snowdrops, and sold as a supplement for lucid dreaming. It raises levels of a brain chemical involved in memory.
descriptions.naloxone: The overdose-reversal drug, sold as Narcan and as a generic nasal spray or injection. It knocks opioids off their receptors and restarts breathing, usually within a few minutes. It does nothing at all to somebody with no opioids in them, which is why it is safe to give when you are not sure. It wears off in 30 to 90 minutes — sooner than most opioids do.
descriptions.clonidine: A blood-pressure medicine also prescribed for ADHD, anxiety, hot flushes and — commonly — to take the edge off opioid withdrawal. It lowers blood pressure and heart rate, so it can cause fainting, and it stacks with anything else that sedates.
descriptions.promethazine: A prescription antihistamine used for nausea, allergies and as a sedative, and the other half of "lean" when mixed with codeine cough syrup. It is heavily sedating on its own and adds to the breathing suppression of opioids.
descriptions.prochlorperazine: A prescription medicine for severe nausea, vomiting and vertigo. It is sedating, and it can cause distressing muscle stiffness and restlessness in a minority of people who take it.
descriptions.quetiapine: An antipsychotic sold as Seroquel, prescribed for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, and very widely prescribed off-label at low doses as a sleeping aid. Strongly sedating.
descriptions.mirtazapine: An antidepressant that is also prescribed for sleep and appetite. Sedating, especially at lower doses. Because it acts on serotonin it carries an interaction risk with MDMA, MAOIs and other antidepressants.
descriptions.risperidone: An antipsychotic prescribed for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and irritability in autism. Sometimes given in emergency rooms to somebody in a drug-induced psychosis.
descriptions.haloperidol: An older antipsychotic, best known as the drug given by injection in emergency rooms to calm somebody agitated or psychotic. It can cause severe muscle stiffness and restlessness.
descriptions.ephedrine: A stimulant from the ephedra plant, sold in the US as an over-the-counter decongestant and asthma medicine, with sales tracked because it can be used to make methamphetamine. It raises heart rate and blood pressure.
descriptions.benzydamine: An anti-inflammatory sold over the counter in many countries as a throat spray, gargle or lozenge for mouth and throat pain. Swallowed in large amounts it causes hallucinations and agitation, which is the only reason it appears here.
descriptions.carisoprodol: A prescription muscle relaxant sold as Soma. Your body converts part of it into meprobamate, an old sedative — which is why it is genuinely habit-forming and why it stacks dangerously with opioids and alcohol.
descriptions.tizanidine: A prescription muscle relaxant for spasms and spasticity. It lowers blood pressure and is sedating.
descriptions.progesterone: A hormone your body makes, also prescribed as a medicine in hormone therapy, contraception and fertility treatment. It is on this list because it changes how the body handles some other drugs, not because it is taken to get high.
descriptions.lisdexamfetamine: Vyvanse — a prescription stimulant for ADHD and binge-eating disorder. It is inactive until your body converts it into dexamfetamine, which is why it comes on gradually and is harder to misuse than other amphetamine pills.
descriptions.dextroamphetamine: A prescription stimulant for ADHD and narcolepsy, and the more active half of Adderall. It increases alertness, focus and heart rate.
descriptions.memantine: A prescription medicine for moderate to severe Alzheimer's disease. It acts on the same receptor as ketamine but far more weakly and much more slowly, and it is not sedating.
descriptions.piracetam: The original "nootropic" — the word was coined for it. Sold as a supplement in the US and prescribed in parts of Europe for cognitive decline and involuntary muscle jerks. Evidence in healthy people is weak.
descriptions.aniracetam: A nootropic in the same family as piracetam, sold as a supplement in the US and as a prescription medicine in some countries. Marketed for memory and anxiety; human evidence is limited.
descriptions.oxiracetam: A nootropic in the piracetam family, sold as a supplement and marketed for memory and focus. Studied mostly in cognitive decline rather than in healthy people.
descriptions.pramiracetam: A nootropic in the piracetam family, sold as a supplement. Marketed for memory; the small amount of research on it is in brain injury, not in healthy people.
descriptions.phenylpiracetam: A nootropic in the piracetam family developed in the Soviet space program, sold as a supplement. Unlike the others it is noticeably stimulating, and it is banned in competitive sport for that reason.
descriptions.adrafinil: A supplement your liver converts into modafinil, the prescription wakefulness drug. It is sold over the counter in the US because it is not itself a controlled substance. The conversion is hard on the liver, which is the main reason to know what it is.
descriptions.methaqualone: Quaaludes — a sedative widely prescribed for sleep in the 1960s and 70s, then banned almost everywhere after widespread misuse. It is essentially absent from the modern supply; pills sold under the name today are usually something else.
descriptions.lsa: The psychedelic compound in morning glory and Hawaiian baby woodrose seeds, which people eat for a long, dreamy, often nauseating experience. Seeds sold for planting are frequently coated with fungicides, and the nausea and vomiting are close to universal.
descriptions.grayanotoxin: The toxin in "mad honey" — honey made from rhododendron nectar, sold from Nepal and Turkey. In small amounts it causes tingling and light-headedness; a little more drops the heart rate and blood pressure hard enough to put people in hospital, which happens regularly.
descriptions.salvinorin-a: The active compound in salvia divinorum, a sage plant, usually smoked as dried leaf. It produces an intense, disorienting experience that is over in minutes and that many people find frightening rather than pleasant. It is not related to any other psychedelic.
descriptions.ibogaine: A compound from the iboga shrub, used in Bwiti ceremonies in Gabon and taken in unregulated clinics abroad as an interruption to opioid dependence. It is not approved anywhere in the US. It disturbs heart rhythm, and deaths in clinic settings are documented — it is not a supervised medical treatment despite being sold as one.
descriptions.inhalants: A category rather than one drug: solvents, glues, aerosols, nitrous oxide, and the alkyl nitrites sold as poppers. What they share is being breathed in for a short high. What they do to the body differs completely between them, and some can stop the heart on a first use.
descriptions.phenobarbital: An old barbiturate, still prescribed for epilepsy and used to manage severe alcohol withdrawal in hospitals. Barbiturates suppress breathing and the gap between an effective amount and a dangerous one is narrow, which is why benzodiazepines replaced them.
descriptions.pentobarbital: A barbiturate once prescribed for sleep, now used mainly in hospitals for anesthesia and seizures, and in veterinary euthanasia. Like all barbiturates it suppresses breathing and the safety margin is narrow.
descriptions.secobarbital: A barbiturate sleeping pill, widely prescribed decades ago and rare now. It suppresses breathing, and mixing it with alcohol is what made it notorious.
descriptions.flunitrazepam: Rohypnol — a strong benzodiazepine sleeping pill, prescribed in some countries and never approved in the US. It is known mainly for drink spiking; the manufacturer added a blue dye for that reason. Like all benzodiazepines it is dangerous alongside opioids or alcohol.
descriptions.midazolam: A short-acting benzodiazepine given in hospitals for sedation before procedures, and to stop prolonged seizures. It works fast and reliably erases memory of the procedure, which is intentional.
descriptions.temazepam: A benzodiazepine prescribed for sleep. Like all benzodiazepines it suppresses breathing alongside opioids and alcohol, and stopping it suddenly after regular use can cause seizures.
descriptions.bromazepam: A benzodiazepine prescribed for anxiety in many countries, though not in the US. Same cautions as the rest of the family: dangerous with opioids and alcohol, and not something to stop abruptly.

education.intro: Nobody is born knowing how to reverse an overdose. These are free, short, and designed for people with no medical background — and some of them come with naloxone in the box at the end.

groups.title: Overdose response and naloxone
groups.blurb: The one to do first. Most take under an hour, several are free and mail you naloxone.

items.name: End Overdose
items.what: Free online certification in opioid overdose response. Their opioid course lists a certificate of completion and a free naloxone kit as what you get for finishing — training and supply in one step. There is also a short game-based version.

items.name: GetNaloxoneNow
items.what: Free online overdose response training, widely used by health departments and often the course a state program points you at.

items.name: NEXT Distro
items.what: Mail-based naloxone. Most states require you to complete their short online training before they ship — that is the norm for free-by-mail programs, not an obstacle they invented.
items.time: Training is brief; shipping takes days

items.name: Your local syringe service program
items.what: In-person training, usually same-day naloxone, and people who can answer questions a website cannot. Often the fastest route if there is one near you.

groups.title: CPR
groups.blurb: Worth having for the overdose where there is no pulse — and for everything else in a life.

items.name: American Red Cross
items.what: In-person, blended and online CPR classes nationwide, with certification.
items.cost: Paid; some community and employer programs cover it

items.name: American Heart Association
items.what: Course finder for AHA CPR training, including Hands-Only CPR, which takes minutes to learn and needs no certification.

groups.title: First aid
groups.blurb: Wounds, bleeding, seizures, and what to do while you wait for help.

items.name: American Red Cross — First Aid

why.title: Do you need training to use naloxone?
why.body: Legally, no — naloxone nasal spray is available over the counter nationwide and you can use it on someone without any certification. Practically, training matters: it is the difference between knowing the steps and working them out while someone is not breathing. It also covers what naloxone does not fix, which is where people get caught out.
why.note: Many free-naloxone programs do ask you to complete a short course before they ship. That is how the supply is funded and tracked — worth doing early rather than on the night you need it.

beforeTheNight.headline: Long nights and hot days
beforeTheNight.blurb: The two that catch people out at an event, before the night rather than during it.

items.t: Overheating, and over-drinking
items.d: Dancing in a hot room you can lose about a pint of water an hour, and stimulants make overheating more likely. Two to three cups an hour — about half a liter — is the ceiling while you are actually dancing, not a target, because past that the water dilutes the sodium in your blood until the brain starts to swell, and at events MDMA is the reason that happens so often. Eat something; food is what keeps your electrolytes where they should be.
items.note: Heat stroke is not the one where they stop sweating — that is the heat wave kind. Somebody having one on a dancefloor is usually still pouring sweat. What tells you is that they stop making sense.

heat.note: Heat illness and water. Three rules if you edit this. (1) The sweating myth is load-bearing: NHS, CDC's traveller page and DanceSafe all say heat stroke means hot dry skin, which describes the heat wave kind, not the dancing kind. NATA's position statement and StatPearls both say exertional heat stroke patients are usually still sweating. If somebody reinstates 'no sweating' here they will teach a reader to rule out the thing that is killing the person in front of them. (2) Ice packs to neck, armpits and groin are near-worthless — 0.028 C/min against the 0.155 that counts as adequate. Most first aid still leads with them. Do not put them back at the top. (3) The fluid ceiling is ~500 mL/h, not the liter this site used to say and most party advice still says; a liter an hour is the whole excretory capacity of a healthy person doing nothing, and MDMA lowers it. See PRIVACY.md rules on denominators — every figure here carries one.
heat.headline: Heat, and water
heat.blurb: How to tell when hot has become dangerous, how to cool somebody down with what is actually in the room, and why drinking too much water swells the brain in people who thought they were being careful.

spot.headline: Telling the difference
spot.lead: Heat exhaustion, drinking too much water and simply being very high on a stimulant share most of their early signs. You are not going to separate them from a symptom list, and neither would a doctor without a blood test. What you are looking for is the one change that decides what you do.

stages.d: Sweating hard, tired, thirsty, a headache starting, cramp in the legs or stomach. They are still making sense. Out of the heat now and it goes no further.
Weak, dizzy, sick, clammy, maybe vomiting, heart going fast. Still lucid — they know where they are and who you are. This is the last rung you can handle yourself.
They stop making sense. Confused, slurring, staggering, unusually aggressive or oddly calm, seizing, or unconscious. This is an ambulance, now.

body: The line between the second rung and the third is not temperature. It is whether they are still thinking straight. Emergency medicine uses the same test: heat stroke is diagnosed on confusion or worse, not on how hot somebody feels to the touch.

Almost every first-aid page you will read says heat stroke means hot, dry skin and no sweating. That describes the kind that happens to an elderly person in a heat wave. The kind that happens to somebody who has been dancing is a different thing, and most people having one are still pouring sweat. If you wait for somebody to stop sweating, you will wait through the entire emergency.

The real threshold is a core temperature around 104°F, and you cannot measure it. Core temperature means a rectal reading. On somebody who has been dancing, an oral thermometer reads roughly 1 to 3°F low and a forehead or armpit one can be off by 2 to 4°F — so a reading of 101°F is entirely compatible with a core of 104. A normal-looking number rules nothing out. Do not spend the time.

emergency.title: Call 911 when they stop making sense
emergency.body: Confusion, slurred speech, staggering, unusual aggression, a seizure, or unconsciousness — in somebody who has been hot, or drinking a lot of water, or both. You do not have to work out which one it is to make the call. It is the same trigger for both. Start cooling while somebody else dials.
emergency.detail: Somebody can seem to come round and then get much worse within minutes. Getting better for a moment is not getting better.

sources.name: NATA position statement — exertional heat illnesses (2015)
Ganio et al., J Athl Train 2009 — validity of non-rectal temperature

cool.headline: Cooling somebody down
cool.lead: With what is in the room. Speed matters more than technique — the harm tracks how long they spend above 104°F, and the target every guideline agrees on is to have them cooled within half an hour of going down.

steps.t: Get them out of the heat
steps.d: Outside, a stairwell, a bathroom, anywhere cooler and away from the crowd. Somebody else calls 911 while you do this. Cooling does not wait for the ambulance to be called, and it does not wait for it to arrive.
As much as the situation allows. Clothing is the insulation you are working against.

steps.t: Cold water on as much skin as you can, and keep it coming
steps.d: A shower, a hose, a bathtub, a sink and a soaked shirt, jugs from behind the bar, ice tipped into water. Not one cold cloth on the forehead — as much surface area as possible, re-wet the moment it stops feeling cold.
steps.note: This is the whole job. Everything else on this list is a detail next to getting a lot of cold water onto a lot of skin.

steps.t: Move air over the wet skin
steps.d: Fan them with a tray, a piece of card, a jacket. Water plus moving air pulls heat out considerably faster than either does alone. Fanning somebody who is dry achieves close to nothing.

steps.t: If you have ice, put it in the right places
steps.d: Cheeks, palms and the soles of the feet. This is the opposite of what most first aid says, and the measurements are not close: ice packs on the neck, armpits and groin move core temperature at about a fifth of the rate that counts as adequate — barely better than doing nothing. Ice is a supplement to soaking them. It is never the plan.
steps.note: If somebody hands you cold packs and nothing else, keep soaking and fanning anyway.

steps.t: Keep going 10 to 15 minutes, then hand over
steps.d: You have no way to measure when they have cooled enough, so use the clock instead. Do not stop early because they seem better — that is the point at which people stop, and it is too soon.
steps.note: Cooling somebody too much is not a realistic risk in fifteen minutes with a bucket. Not cooling them enough is the one that happens.

never.title: What not to do
items: Do not give acetaminophen, ibuprofen or aspirin. This is not a fever and they do nothing for it — the body's thermostat is not what has gone wrong. They can make the liver damage and the bleeding problems worse.
Do not hold somebody down. Straining against being held generates heat, and it is one of the reliable ways to make overheating worse in somebody on a stimulant. Clear the space around them instead.
Do not pour drink into somebody who is confused, drowsy or being sick. They can inhale it — and if too much water is the actual problem, you are making it worse.
Do not treat drinking as cooling. Fluids do not bring core temperature down.
Do not delay cooling to take a temperature you cannot take accurately.

sources.name: McDermott et al., J Athl Train 2009 — cooling rates compared
DeMartini et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc 2015 — 274 consecutive patients, no deaths
BC Emergency Health Services — hyperthermia guideline

water.headline: The other way this goes wrong
water.lead: "Drink water" is the most repeated piece of advice at any event, and the version people act on — drink constantly, drink more if you feel bad — is the version that has put them in intensive care.
body: Your kidneys can only get rid of so much water: somewhere around a liter an hour at the absolute best, in a healthy person with nothing else going on. Stimulants and MDMA stop your body clearing it properly. Drink past what you can pass and the sodium in your blood dilutes, cells swell, and the cells with nowhere to swell into are the ones in your skull.

In four pooled trials, 96 healthy adults were given an ordinary dose of MDMA in a lab — sitting still, air conditioned, drinking as much or as little as they wanted. Among those left to drink freely, 37% became hyponatremic. Among the 15 whose fluids were limited, none did. Nobody in that study was dancing, and nobody was in a hot room.

items.t: What it looks like
items.d: The early signs are the heat exhaustion signs — headache, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, confusion. Three things belong to this one and not to heat: they look puffy, especially the fingers and the face, and rings or shoes feel tight; they have gained weight rather than lost it after hours of exertion; and they have not urinated in a long time despite drinking steadily.
items.note: The most useful thing you have is not a sign, it is the story. If somebody has been drinking water for hours, say that to the medics out loud. It is what makes a clinician check their sodium instead of treating them for something else.

items.t: What to do
items.d: Stop the fluids. All of them, including sports drinks. If they are fully awake and not vomiting, salty food is the right thing — salt without water is exactly what they need. Sit them somewhere cool and stay with them.

items.t: It can arrive hours later
items.d: Symptoms can start within 24 hours of leaving, in somebody who seemed fine on the way out. Do not let them go home alone to sleep it off. Tell them, and tell whoever they are with, what to watch for.

emergency.title: This one is also 911
emergency.body: A seizure, confusion or drowsiness, vomiting with a bad headache, trouble breathing, or frothy spit. It is the same trigger as heat stroke — they stop making sense. The difference is what you do next: cool them, but do not give them anything to drink.

water.note: Being honest about the size of this: more people die of overheating at events than of over-drinking, by a wide margin. What makes water intoxication worth its own section is that it turns into a 911 emergency in people who believed they were doing the careful thing.

sources.name: Hew-Butler et al. — 3rd International Exercise-Associated Hyponatremia Consensus (2015)
Atila et al., JAMA Netw Open 2024 — MDMA and hyponatremia, 4 pooled trials
Rosenson et al., J Emerg Med 2007 — MDMA hyponatremia case series

items.t: Two to three cups an hour, not four
items.d: About half a liter an hour while you are actually dancing, and less when you are not. That is lower than most party advice, including the number this site used to give. A liter an hour is the entire amount a healthy person's kidneys can clear while doing nothing at all — it was never a safety ceiling, it was an estimate of how much a dancer sweats — and MDMA lowers what you can clear.
items.note: People have become seriously ill at intakes as low as about two cups an hour. There is no volume that is guaranteed safe; there is only less risk.

items.t: Thirst is a better guide than a schedule
items.d: Thirst tracks what your body actually needs. The advice to get ahead of it came out of workplaces and endurance sport, and in dance settings it is the specific instruction that has put people in hospital — in the case reports "stay ahead of thirst" keeps coming back from the people who followed it. Losing up to about 3% of your body weight in fluid does you no harm.

sources.name: Hew-Butler et al. — EAH consensus, drinking behavior

items.t: Electrolyte drinks do less than they sound like they do
items.d: Every sports drink is more dilute than your blood, so it still adds free water faster than it adds salt. Better than the same volume of plain water, but it does not buy permission to drink more, and it will not prevent this. Volume is what hurts you. Salty food is the thing that moves sodium without adding more water to clear.

items.t: Get off the floor before you need to
items.d: In a study that measured real clubs — 29°C and 90% humidity among the dancers — an hour of dancing raised core temperature by 1.8°C, and four hours without a break modeled out to 39.1°C. Twenty minutes somewhere cooler, before anything is wrong, does more for you than anything you can drink.

sources.name: McNeill & Parsons — Heat stress in night-clubs (1996)

risk.headline: Who it hits hardest

items.t: The first few days in it
items.d: This is the best-evidenced item on the page and the one nobody mentions. Your body adapts to heat over about one to two weeks, and it loses that adaptation within days of not being in it. OSHA's figures on heat deaths at work: more than 70% happen in somebody's first week, and close to half on their first day, or their first day back after time away.
items.note: It is not about being fit or being used to hard work. It is about how recently your body was last doing this in this heat.

sources.name: OSHA — protecting new and returning workers
Daanen et al., Sports Med 2018 — how fast heat acclimatization decays

items.t: Not being able to go somewhere cooler
items.d: The single largest risk factor is having nowhere to get out of it. Across Las Vegas and Los Angeles, researchers estimated that half of all deaths among people experiencing homelessness in Clark County were attributable to temperature — a figure they described as orders of magnitude above the general population. In Maricopa County, Arizona, 208 of the 430 heat deaths recorded in 2025 were among people who were unhoused.
items.note: Of the indoor heat deaths in that county, 94% happened in homes that had air conditioning. In 72% of those, it was not running — broken, or shut off because of the bill.

sources.name: Lin et al., Am J Epidemiol 2024 — temperature-attributable mortality among people experiencing homelessness

items.t: Using drugs in a heat wave
items.d: Of the 430 heat deaths in Maricopa County in 2025, 236 involved substances, and 194 of those involved a stimulant. That is a count of who died, not a rate — it cannot tell you how much more likely it is. The one study that measured the risk properly, across the 2021 heat dome in British Columbia, found substance use disorder raised the odds of dying by about a quarter. Real, but smaller than you might expect, and much smaller than being poor, which roughly doubled them.
items.note: Stimulants raise the heat your body makes and how long you stay in it. Both matter more in a heat wave than on a dancefloor, because a heat wave lasts days.

sources.name: McLean et al., Environ Res Health 2024 — deaths in the 2021 BC heat dome

items.t: Medication, with a caveat about how sure anyone is
items.d: The standard warning list is longer than the evidence for it. When researchers pooled 35 heat-stress experiments, only strong anticholinergics and non-selective beta blockers actually raised core temperature; antidepressants, antihistamines and antipsychotics did not. But the real-world data disagrees with the lab: among older adults, heat waves plus antipsychotics, loop diuretics or anticholinergics meant clearly more heat hospitalizations, and during the BC heat dome, people with schizophrenia taking antipsychotics had roughly 2.4 times the odds of dying.
items.note: The one with a warning printed on the label is topiramate, sold as Topamax and used for seizures and migraine: it can reduce sweating, most often in children. Do not stop a prescribed medication over this. Take the heat more seriously instead.

sources.name: Hospers et al., eClinicalMedicine 2024 — meta-analysis of 35 heat-stress trials
Layton et al., PLoS One 2020 — medications and heat hospitalization in 9,721 people
Chen et al., Sci Rep 2025 — antipsychotics and death in the BC heat dome

items.t: Alcohol, and what is actually wrong with it
items.d: Not what you have been told. A review of eight studies found alcohol did not reduce sweating and did not raise core temperature — the dehydration only showed up at the highest doses tested. The link between drinking and dying in heat waves is real and well documented; what has never been studied is the obvious explanation, which is that drinking changes whether you notice you are in trouble and whether you do anything about it.
items.note: Worth saying plainly: this is a gap in the research, not a finding. Treat alcohol in heat as a reason to have somebody watching out for you rather than as something that dries you out.

sources.name: Morris et al., Environ Health 2024 — alcohol and thermoregulation, scoping review

items.t: Smaller bodies have less room for error
items.d: Less total body water means a given surplus moves your sodium further. In the MDMA case reports the skew is stark — in one poison-center series of 73 people with hyponatremia, 55 were women, and women had about four times the odds of it. Some of that is body size and some is how much people drink, but it is not nothing.
items.note: This is not a reason for anyone else to relax. It means the margin is narrower if you are small, not that it is wide if you are not.

sources.name: Rosenson et al., J Emerg Med 2007

items.t: Hours, not doses
items.d: In 488 runners tested at the end of a marathon, 13% were hyponatremic. The things that predicted it were gaining weight during the race and being out there more than four hours — not sex, and not what they drank. Time spent in it is the exposure.

sources.name: Almond et al., N Engl J Med 2005 — hyponatremia among marathon runners

risk.lead: Two of the things on this list are much better established than the advice you will have heard, and two are much weaker. Both are worth knowing, because acting on the weak ones instead of the strong ones is how people get caught out.

index.disclaimer: Aggregated from public reporting and not independently verified. Many changes in local drug supply are never publicly announced, and reporting lags reality. No alerts does not mean a safe supply.

market.note: HAND-WRITTEN. Explains the MECHANICS of an unregulated supply — why potency varies, why adulterants appear, why the same source is not the same product. Deliberately contains NOTHING that helps anyone buy: no marketplaces, no vendor guidance, no sourcing, no advice on avoiding detection while purchasing. That line is the difference between harm reduction and a buying guide.
market.headline: Why the supply is like this
market.intro: Most harm reduction advice is a list of rules. This is the reason behind them — because the rules make more sense, and stick better, once you know what is actually happening to the drugs before they reach you.

blocks.title: Enforcement pushes drugs toward stronger, smaller forms
blocks.body: This has a name: the Iron Law of Prohibition. When a supply is squeezed, the economics favor whatever is most compact — a trafficker faces roughly the same penalty for a small package as a large one, so potency per unit of volume goes up. That is the path the US market has taken: prescription pills to heroin, heroin to fentanyl, and now fentanyl to nitazenes. Each step is smaller, stronger, and harder to dose.
blocks.sotu: It also explains why cracking down on one drug so reliably produces a stronger replacement, rather than less supply.

sources.name: Beletsky & Davis — Prohibition’s Iron Law, revisited (Int J Drug Policy, 2017)

blocks.title: Potency is an accident of mixing, not a recipe
blocks.body: Fentanyl is active in microgram amounts. Mixing micrograms evenly through a kilogram of powder is an industrial process, and this is not an industrial process. What reaches you was cut and re-cut by people without equipment to do it evenly, so two bags off the same batch can differ, and so can two ends of the same bag.
blocks.sotu: This is the whole reason “start with much less than usual” is the first rule, and why testing a dissolved portion of everything beats testing a pinch.

blocks.title: Adulterants are added for reasons that have nothing to do with you
blocks.body: Xylazine lengthens a short fentanyl high, which makes a supply feel more like heroin and reduces how often someone needs to buy. Levamisole and lidocaine bulk out cocaine and mimic its numbing. Caffeine and diphenhydramine are cheap filler. None of these are chosen for effect on the person taking them — they are chosen for cost, weight, and how the product behaves in a market.
blocks.sotu: Which is why the adulterant in your supply can change without anything about your source changing.

blocks.title: A trusted source is not a quality control system
blocks.body: The person selling to you is usually near the end of a long chain and did not make what they are selling. They can be completely honest with you and still not know what is in it — most people at that end of the chain are using the same supply themselves. Trust tells you about a person. It tells you nothing about a batch.
blocks.sotu: This is the single most common way people are caught out: the supply changed, the source did not.

blocks.title: Ratings and “lab tested” claims are not verification
blocks.body: Buying through a screen adds review scores, vendor histories and sometimes a photographed lab report — the visual furniture of a regulated market. None of it is verification. A rating measures whether previous orders arrived and matched a description, which is a delivery record, not a chemical one. A lab report can be real and still describe a different batch than the one in your hand, or belong to someone else entirely, or be edited.
blocks.sotu: Every earlier point on this page still applies: the person selling is rarely the person who made it, potency still varies within a batch, and nobody in the chain tested what you received.

blocks.title: Counterfeit pills are the sharpest version of this
blocks.body: A pressed pill looks finished and identical to the next one, which is exactly what makes it dangerous — it carries the visual signals of a regulated product with none of the process behind them. Pill presses do not distribute a microgram-scale drug evenly, so within a single batch one pill can hold a survivable amount and the next several times that.
blocks.sotu: An imprint, a color, and a shape can all be copied. None of them are evidence of what is inside.

blocks.title: Distance does not change the chemistry
blocks.body: It is easy to believe a supply that arrives in the mail is cleaner than one bought in person — better presented, more anonymous, further from anyone you might blame. The adulterants that matter get added early, near production, long before anything is packaged or listed. Where the last handover happened does not change what is in the powder.
blocks.sotu: Which is why a sample you did not test yourself is an unknown regardless of how it reached you.

close.title: What follows from all of this
close.body: None of it is a reason to despair, and none of it makes anything safe. It is the reasoning behind four things that measurably lower the odds: assume a new batch is stronger than the last one, test what you can, take much less than you plan to at first, and do not be alone. Those are not rules handed down. They are what the mechanics above actually imply.

scope.title: What this page deliberately leaves out
scope.body: Nothing here explains where to buy, which sellers to use, or how to avoid being caught doing it. That is not squeamishness — it is that none of it would make anyone safer. Every risk on this page comes from what is in the drugs, and no purchasing decision changes that. What changes it is testing, dose, and not being alone.

name-warnings.note: Street names that MISLEAD - the name says one drug, the market sells another. Renders as a warning on the substance page and the names become searchable aliases. Every entry needs a live-verified source; this file exists because a name can be the adulteration vector.

2c-b.text: “Tusi” and “pink cocaine” sound like this substance — they almost never are it. Of 960 pink powders DEA seized since 2020, only 4 contained any 2C-B. The pink powder sold under these names is typically a ketamine mix, often with MDMA or caffeine, and sometimes opioids. It also usually contains no cocaine. If it is pink powder, treat it as an unknown ketamine blend, not as 2C-B.

calling.headline: If you call 911, what happens to you?
calling.lead: This is the question that stops people, and it deserves a real answer rather than reassurance.
body: Fear of police is the most commonly documented reason people don't call for help during an overdose. That fear is not irrational, and telling you it is would be dishonest.

Every state, plus DC, now has a Good Samaritan overdose law. New Mexico was first in 2007; Kansas and Wyoming were the last, in 2024 and 2025. But what those laws actually protect varies enormously, and the gaps are the part nobody tells you.

limits.headline: What these laws generally do not cover

items.t: Being arrested
items.d: Only 25 states and DC explicitly protect against arrest or being taken into custody. In roughly half the country the law protects you from being prosecuted, and says nothing about being handcuffed first.

items.t: Anything beyond possession
items.d: Protection is generally limited to low-level possession and paraphernalia. 39 states and DC expressly include paraphernalia. Selling, sharing, or handing someone drugs is usually excluded outright.

items.t: A homicide charge
items.d: 35 states plus DC have a drug-induced homicide law, and Good Samaritan protection reaches that charge in only three: Kentucky, Vermont, and Virginia. Someone who used alongside a person who died has been charged with homicide after calling for help. In most states the Good Samaritan law does not stop that.

items.t: An outstanding warrant
items.d: Not protected. In 12 states and DC, acting in good faith expressly excludes seeking help while a warrant is being executed.

items.t: Probation or parole
items.d: Only 27 states and DC extend protection to a violation. 23 states do not.

items.t: Evidence of other crimes
items.d: 31 states and DC specify that immunity is not grounds for suppressing evidence of something else found at the scene.

variations.headline: Where your state changes the answer entirely

items.t: Texas and Utah
items.d: An affirmative defense, not immunity. That means it is raised at trial, after you have been charged — not a reason you don't get charged.

items.t: Alabama, Indiana, Maine, Oklahoma, Wisconsin
items.d: The caller is protected. The person who overdosed is not. Louisiana is the reverse.

items.t: Alabama, Iowa, North Carolina, South Carolina, Texas
items.d: Only the first person to call is covered.

items.t: Indiana
items.d: The only state that requires the caller to administer naloxone.

variations.note: Most laws also require you to call in good faith, stay on the scene, and cooperate with responders. Leaving can cost you the protection.

calling.bottom: None of this is a reason not to call. It is the reason to know what your state actually does before you are standing over someone. Look it up before you need it, not while you need it.

sources.name: LAPPA — Good Samaritan Fatal Overdose Prevention and Drug-Induced Homicide: Summary of State Laws (research current July 2025)
GAO-21-248 — Most States Have Good Samaritan Laws (2021)

law.headline: Where the law actually stands
law.blurb: Dated, because all of this moves. Anything here without a date should be treated as unverified.

items.t: Fentanyl test strips are legal almost everywhere — but not quite
items.d: As of July 1 2026, possessing drug-checking equipment is outside paraphernalia law in 47 states, DC and 4 territories. Three states still potentially reach it: Iowa, North Dakota, Texas. Strips for xylazine are narrower — 11 more states wrote their carve-out for fentanyl only, so it does not cover xylazine there. Florida and Wisconsin cover fentanyl and xylazine but not medetomidine or nitazene strips.

sources.name: LAPPA — Drug Checking Equipment fact sheet, July 2026

items.t: Federal money stopped paying for test strips in April 2026
items.d: HHS guidance dated April 24 2026 bars federal funding from buying or distributing syringes, safer smoking supplies, sterile water, and test strips of any kind — including fentanyl, xylazine and medetomidine. Test strips were explicitly fundable as recently as July 2025. Naloxone, wound care, sharps disposal, condoms and HIV/HCV testing are still funded. Legal to own is not the same as available near you, and this is why the two can diverge.

items.t: Xylazine and medetomidine are not federally scheduled
items.d: Neither is a controlled substance as of August 2026. Both are veterinary sedatives. Nine states have scheduled xylazine on their own. Medetomidine reports to federal forensic labs went from 12 in 2021 to 8,391 in 2025.

sources.name: DEA Diversion Control — Xylazine fact sheet, May 2026
DEA Diversion Control — Medetomidine fact sheet, March 2026

items.t: Fentanyl-related substances are permanently Schedule I as a class
items.d: The HALT Fentanyl Act became law on July 16 2025. It controls fentanyl-like compounds by chemical structure rather than one at a time, and extends the same mandatory minimums — 400 grams for ten years, 40 grams for five. Supporters say it stops traffickers from changing one molecule to stay legal. Critics, including civil rights and drug policy organizations, say it schedules substances without individual evidence of harm and sweeps in compounds that may be inert. The Sentencing Commission added a rebuttable exception, effective November 1 2026, for substances shown to be significantly less potent than fentanyl or to counteract it.

sources.name: Public Law 119-26 (HALT Fentanyl Act), enacted July 16 2025

items.t: Cannabis rescheduling is half-done, and the main question is undecided
items.d: A final rule effective April 28 2026 moved cannabis to Schedule III only where it is in an FDA-approved drug product or under a state medical license. Everything else, including all adult-use cannabis, stays Schedule I. A separate hearing on whether cannabis generally should move concluded July 15 2026; briefs were not due until August 17 2026 and no decision has issued. Three petitions challenging the rule are pending in the D.C. Circuit. Anyone telling you the outcome right now is guessing.

items.t: Syringe programs: federal funds still cannot buy the syringes
items.d: A rider carried in every appropriations act, including the one enacted February 3 2026, bars federal money from buying needles or syringes anywhere. Federal funds can support the rest of a program — staff, testing, naloxone, referrals — but only where a health department has made a determination of need with CDC. 37 states, DC and Puerto Rico authorize syringe programs; roughly 587 were operating as of June 2026. Five states have none at all: Kansas, Mississippi, Nebraska, South Dakota, Wyoming.

items.t: Overdose prevention centers: two operating, contested federally
items.d: Two sanctioned programs operate in the US — OnPoint NYC's two locations in Manhattan, and one in Providence run by Project Weber/RENEW, which Rhode Island authorized by statute and extended to March 1 2028. Vermont has authorized one that has not opened. Federal law, 21 U.S.C. 856, makes maintaining a place for drug use an offense, and an executive order signed July 24 2025 directs review of federally funded organizations operating such sites. No prosecution of an operating site is documented. The pressure so far has been money: OnPoint reported losing over $2 million in federal grants.

sources.name: Rhode Island Department of Health — harm reduction centers

items.t: Overdose deaths have fallen four years running — but not everywhere
items.d: CDC's provisional counts show 67,798 deaths in the 12 months ending March 2026, down 12.3% year over year and below the 2019 figure, from a peak of 110,393 in 2022. Seven jurisdictions rose over that period rather than fell, led by New Mexico at +28.3%, Colorado at +11.6% and Arizona at +5.3%. A national decline is not your county's decline.

sources.name: CDC/NCHS — Provisional Drug Overdose Death Counts (data updated August 12 2026)

money.headline: Follow the money
money.blurb: Where the funding actually comes from, and why that decides what exists near you.
body: Roughly $58.6 billion in opioid settlement money is being paid to state and local governments over 18 years, with payments having started in 2022. Settlement agreements generally require 85% to go to opioid remediation.

How it is being spent is documented and uneven. About $6 billion was distributed through 2023. Of the roughly $2.2 billion of that which jurisdictions actually reported spending, syringe services received 1.7% — about $37.3 million — while 41.3% went to an “other” bucket that mixes law enforcement with treatment workforce and multi-category spending. These are 2022–23 expenditures released in December 2024, and the database itself is described as incomplete. Roughly a third was appropriated, a third held in reserve, and a third is unaccounted for because some jurisdictions have not reported at all.
Of twelve states that committed in writing to disclose every dollar, seven had kept that commitment by late 2024. Four jurisdictions — Alaska, DC, Louisiana and Mississippi — had published nothing.

This is the most direct lever most people have. Settlement spending is decided by state and county officials, in public processes, and it is now the main legal channel for the supplies federal money stopped covering in April 2026.
