practice.note: HAND-WRITTEN. Practice exercises, not a quiz. There is no score, no timer, no streak and no fail state anywhere in this file, and adding one would break the thing it is for. Content mirrors the real guidance in site/js/views/help.js and data/testing.json — if those change, this must change with them.
practice.intro: Reading how to do something and being able to do it at 3am are different. These let you practice, with nothing riding on it.

strip.title: Read the strip
strip.why: One line means positive. That is backwards from every other test people have used, and it is the single most misread result in drug checking. Worth getting wrong here, where it costs nothing.

cards.alt: A test strip showing one line, in the control area only.
cards.right: One line is POSITIVE — fentanyl is in the sample.
cards.explain: The strip works by competition: fentanyl in the sample blocks the test line from forming. The drug being present makes a line disappear. That is why it reads backwards from a pregnancy test.

cards.alt: A test strip showing two lines.
cards.right: Two lines is NEGATIVE — nothing detected in what you tested.
cards.explain: A second line can be very faint and still count as negative. Wait the full time your instructions give before deciding — a faint line can appear and then fade. And a negative is about the sample you dissolved, not the rest of the bag.

cards.alt: A test strip showing no lines at all.
cards.right: No lines means the test failed — it tells you nothing.
cards.explain: No lines, or a line only on the end you dipped, means the strip did not run properly. Too much liquid, too little, or a bad strip. Use a new one; do not read it as negative.

overdose.title: Walk through an overdose
overdose.why: The order matters more than people expect, and it changed recently. Nothing here is timed and nothing is scored — take as long as you want on each one.

steps.scene: Someone is slumped over and not moving. You are the only person there.

options.label: Look at their chest for breathing
Shake them and shout their name

steps.right: Breathing first. Look at their chest.
steps.explain: This changed in 2025. Sedatives now common in the supply — xylazine, medetomidine — can leave someone impossible to wake while their breathing is fine. Checking whether they respond first can mislead you in both directions. Bad breathing or no response, either one, means act.

onWrong.shake: Reasonable, and it used to be step one. But someone can be unwakeable and breathing fine on a sedative — the chest tells you more than the shoulder does.
onWrong.call: You will call, and soon. But look at their chest first so you can tell the dispatcher whether they are breathing, which is the thing that changes what happens next.
onWrong.naloxone: Not wrong, and if it is already in your hand it costs seconds. But look at the chest first — you need to know what you are treating and whether it is working.

steps.scene: Their breathing is slow and sounds like snoring. They do not wake when you shout or rub their breastbone.

options.label: Wait a few minutes to see if they come to
Try to walk them around or give them a cold shower
Put them to bed on their side and check later

steps.explain: Snoring or gurgling breathing is an obstructed airway, not sleep. If you are alone and naloxone is in your hand, give it first, then call — with two people, one calls while the other doses.

onWrong.wait: Waiting is the thing that does the damage here. Lack of oxygen is what causes it, and it is happening while you wait.
onWrong.coffee: These do not work and they waste the minutes that do. Cold water and walking cannot make someone breathe.
onWrong.sleep: Leaving someone in this state is how the airway closes the rest of the way and the breathing stops, with nobody in the room. Snoring here is the airway, not sleep.

steps.scene: You gave one dose of naloxone. Two minutes later their breathing is better but they are still asleep and confused.

options.label: It worked — watch them and stay
It failed — give more doses until they wake up
They are stable now, so you can head off

steps.right: It worked. Breathing is the measure, not waking.
steps.explain: Judge by their chest, not their eyes. Someone can stay asleep after a reversal that already worked — that is the sedative, not a failed dose. Naloxone wears off in 30–90 minutes and most opioids last longer, so they can go under again.

onWrong.more: Understandable, but stacking doses to force someone awake can throw them into hard withdrawal for no gain. If breathing improved, it worked.
onWrong.leave: This is the most common fatal mistake after a successful reversal. Naloxone wears off before the drug does, and if you have gone, no one is there when their breathing drops again.

steps.scene: A different night. You gave naloxone, breathing improved, but they are still deeply sedated — and you know tranq is around.
steps.ask: What does naloxone do about the xylazine?

options.label: Nothing — but you still give it
Skip naloxone if you think it is xylazine

steps.right: Nothing for the xylazine — and you give it anyway.
steps.explain: Xylazine and medetomidine are not opioids, so naloxone cannot lift their sedation. It still reverses the fentanyl that is almost always with them, and the fentanyl is what stops breathing. Watch their breathing rather than whether they wake up.

onWrong.reverses: It does not — they are alpha-2 agonists, a different receptor entirely. That is why someone stays sedated after a reversal that worked.
onWrong.skip: This is the dangerous version of knowing about xylazine. Skipping naloxone leaves the fentanyl unreversed, and the fentanyl is the part that stops breathing.

close.title: That is the whole protocol
close.body: Breathing first. Naloxone even when unsure. Judge by the chest. Stay. If you want the full version with sources, it is on the Emergency tab — and a real course with a certificate, often with free naloxone at the end, is one tap away below.

regional.headline: There is no single American drug supply. There are at least four.
regional.summary: Of 90 drugs detected routinely in mail-in drug checking, only 20 turn up everywhere at similar rates. The other 70 are concentrated — some 80 to 90 percent confined to a single region. A drug is counted as regional when one region holds at least 35% of its national signal.
regional.caveat: This is not a random sample of the US drug supply. It is what reaches harm reduction programs and drug-checking partners, and that coverage is uneven — strong in some states, thin in others.

rx.note: HAND-CURATED, every claim live-verified against the cited source on lastVerified date. Confidence is stated per claim; 'no reliable source' entries are deliberate - an honest gap beats an invented severity. FDA's 2016/2017 Drug Safety Communication pages have rotted (404); claims anchor to DailyMed labels, live FDA pages, and SAMHSA TIP 63 instead.
rx.intro: If you take prescribed medication and also use other drugs, the prescription changes the math. None of this is a reason to stop a medication - stopping methadone or bupe abruptly is its own danger. It is a reason to know which combinations carry documented risk.

items.with: Benzos, alcohol, other opioids, any depressant
items.claim: Boxed warning: profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, death. This is the label's strongest warning, not fine print.

items.with: Using benzos while on methadone treatment
items.claim: Federal guidance says treatment should not be withheld or stopped over benzodiazepine use - it should be managed. If a program threatens to cut you off, that is not what the guidance says.
Methadone carries a boxed warning for life-threatening heart rhythm changes (QT prolongation); the risk adds up with other drugs that do the same.
Boosters can change methadone levels - worth a per-pair check.
Label warning: serious risk including death, especially with injection or misuse. Same rule as methadone: this is managed, not a reason to lose treatment.

Precipitated withdrawal risk is real and highest within 24-48 hours of fentanyl use - in one study of 1,679 people, 22% had severe withdrawal starting under 24 hours. This is observational evidence, not a trial.

items.with: Using fentanyl or heroin on top of bupe
items.claim: Higher bupe doses blunt other opioids' effects. That is pharmacology, not protection - it is not overdose-proof.

items.with: Opioids after a missed dose or stopping
items.claim: The label warns of heightened overdose vulnerability: tolerance drops during treatment, and trying to push through the blockade with a large amount is what stops breathing.

Labels list amphetamines among drugs with serotonin syndrome risk. Separately, a controlled human study found SSRIs blunt most of MDMA's effect - which people sometimes chase with more. Neither fact makes the mix predictable.
Contraindicated on every label, with documented severe reactions - this is the serotonergic combination with the worst record.
Tramadol's label carries both a serotonin syndrome warning and a seizure warning, and both risks rise when combined with SSRIs/SNRIs.
Class-wide boxed warning: combined use risks profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, death.
Oral midazolam and triazolam are contraindicated with boosters, and some other benzo levels rise. Check the specific pair.
Boosters block the enzyme that clears fentanyl, raising exposure and respiratory-depression risk.
Documented deaths and near-deaths with ritonavir - one MDMA fatality showed roughly ten times the expected blood level. Case reports, not rates; the mechanism is strong.
Use the Liverpool checker for the specific pair - it is the specialist resource, kept current, and free.
PrEP itself is not a booster - its label lists no recreational-drug interactions. The interaction concern belongs to boosted treatment regimens, not PrEP. That is 'none listed', not 'proven none'.

rx.unresolved: Combinations we could not find reliable evidence for, stated so nobody mistakes silence for safety: methadone + stimulants (severity), SSRIs + cocaine, naltrexone + stimulants, buprenorphine + stimulants, and how often SSRI + MDMA actually causes serotonin syndrome (the label states the risk; the frequency is unknown).

sex.note: Hand-curated. Written for people who are going to be out, using, and having sex, because that is what happens. Nothing here is conditional on stopping any of it.
sex.headline: Sexual health
sex.blurb: Barriers, PrEP and PEP, emergency contraception, the drug interactions that actually put people in the hospital, and an honest answer about drink testing.

framing.headline: Why this page is not a list of precautions
body: The usual nightlife advice — watch your drink, don't go out alone, don't wear that — has a measured effect, and it is not the one intended.

In a review of research on preventing sexual harm in nightlife, people who were given victim-focused prevention tips went on to blame victims MORE than people given tips aimed at potential perpetrators. Only 8 of 35 studies evaluated whether an intervention worked at all.
So this page is built the other way around: what you can do for other people, what actually reduces risk, and what to do afterwards.

sources.name: Button et al., Archives of Sexual Behavior 2024

spiking.headline: Drink spiking, honestly
spiking.blurb: Not what the posters say, and the products sold for it mostly do not work.

items.t: The drug most likely to be involved is alcohol
items.d: In a US study of 144 people reporting sexual assault, drugs were found in 61.8% — but only 4.9% were the classic “date-rape” drugs, and 4.2% were assessed as having been drugged without knowing. In 100 people at an Oslo clinic who suspected spiking, GHB was found in exactly none. Across the research, the substance most often involved is alcohol, sometimes more of it than the person ordered.
items.note: This is not a reason to relax. It is a reason to point your attention at the right thing — how much you have actually had, and who is topping you up.

items.t: Drink test strips and coasters mostly do not work
items.d: Detection coasters showed 0% sensitivity for ketamine in laboratory testing, and their “GHB” reagent turned out to be bromocresol green — a pH indicator that responds to any drink above about pH 5.5, not to GHB. Consumer kits tested at 37.5% and 69% sensitivity. In the strongest test, 236 drinks collected from real venues were clean by mass spectrometry across 39 drugs, and the color kits called up to 97% of them positive.
items.note: Massachusetts' health department reviewed these and recommended against buying and distributing them. California, meanwhile, requires bars to offer them — and in the same law immunizes everyone against a wrong result. A state mandate is not an efficacy finding.

sources.name: Germain et al., Forensic Sci Int 2023
Gautam & Grela, Anglia Ruskin University for Drinkaware, 2024

items.t: A cover is different, and worth using
items.d: Nobody has tested whether drink covers work — that is a real gap, not a hidden finding. But a cover cannot give you a false negative. A strip can tell you your drink is clear when it is not, and that is worse than having nothing.
items.note: That distinction is the whole point: prefer the thing that cannot lie to you.

items.t: If you think it happened
items.d: Urine is worth collecting up to 96 hours after, which is longer than most sources say — sooner is much better, and the first time you pee is the best sample. You do not have to decide about police to have evidence taken, and the exam must not be made conditional on agreeing to a toxicology test. The National Sexual Assault Hotline is 800-656-4673.
items.note: Voluntary drug use does not make it not an assault, and does not disqualify a case. The federal examination protocol says so directly to clinicians.

sources.name: US DOJ — National Protocol for Sexual Assault Medical Forensic Examinations

items.t: And the other direction
items.d: In a survey of 6,064 students, 462 reported having been drugged — and 83 reported drugging someone else. Men who did it most often gave “having fun” as the reason. Giving somebody a drug they are not expecting is never a joke, whatever it was.

sources.name: Swan et al., Psychology of Violence 2017

items.t: Condoms, and what actually breaks them
items.d: About 98% effective with perfect use and around 87% in real life — meaning roughly 13 of every 100 people using them as their only birth control get pregnant in a year. Breakage is about 2 per 100 condoms; failure is usually about use rather than the rubber.
items.note: New one every time, on before any genital contact, pinch the air out of the tip, hold the base coming out. Not in a wallet, not two at once, never past the expiry.

items.t: Oil destroys latex, fast
items.d: Mineral oil cut condom strength by around 90% after sixty seconds of contact. Baby oil dropped the average burst time from nearly a minute to just over eleven seconds. Water- or silicone-based only, with latex AND with polyisoprene. Polyurethane is the exception that tolerates oil.
items.note: Lambskin is for pregnancy only — its pores are more than ten times the diameter of HIV.

items.t: Internal condoms, and one hard rule
items.d: About 95% with perfect use, around 79% typical. They can be used for anal sex, though the evidence for that specifically is described as unknown. Used at the same time as an external condom, the friction tears both.

items.t: Dental dams
items.d: The CDC recommends them and gives instructions, including how to cut one from a condom. Worth saying plainly: nobody has ever measured how much risk they remove. We are not going to borrow a condom's number for them.

items.t: Long sessions
items.d: Friction over hours causes sores and bleeding, which is how HIV and hepatitis get passed on during sessions that were meant to be safe. Plenty of water-based lube, and a new condom every 30 minutes rather than every act.

sources.name: We Are With You — chemsex harm reduction

items.t: PEP is an emergency, and the clock is 72 hours
items.d: If you think you were exposed to HIV — sex, a shared needle, an assault — post-exposure prophylaxis works if started within 72 hours, ideally within 24. It is a 28-day course. Go to an emergency room or urgent care and say you need PEP. It is started before any test results come back — the 72-hour clock matters more than the confirmation does.
items.note: In twelve states pharmacists can prescribe it directly: Arkansas, California, Colorado, Illinois, Maine, Nevada, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Oregon, Utah and Virginia.

items.t: PrEP, and how long before it protects you
items.d: Daily pills, a shot every two months, or a shot twice a year. Around 99% risk reduction from sex and at least 74% for injecting. It is not immediate: roughly 7 days of daily pills for receptive anal sex, and around 21 days for receptive vaginal sex and for injecting.
items.note: CDC does not recommend the on-demand “2-1-1” schedule — it is not FDA approved and there is no data for people who inject, for women, or for trans people.

items.t: Recreational drugs do not interfere with most PrEP
items.d: This is the reassuring one and it is real: there are no known interactions between recreational drugs and the daily PrEP pills or the shot every two months. The exception is the twice-yearly lenacapavir shot, which does affect how the body clears other drugs.

sources.name: aidsmap — interactions between HIV medication and recreational drugs

items.t: Testing, and how often
items.d: Anyone sharing injecting equipment: HIV at least once a year. Men who have sex with men: syphilis, chlamydia and gonorrhea at least yearly at every site of contact regardless of condom use, and every 3 to 6 months with multiple partners — including if you are on PrEP. Free and low-cost testing is findable at gettested.cdc.gov.

items.t: What you can get, and by when
items.d: Levonorgestrel (Plan B and generics) is over the counter with no age limit and no ID, and works best within 72 hours. Ulipristal (ella) needs a prescription and works up to 120 hours. A copper IUD fitted within 120 hours is the most effective option there is — better than 99% — and works as well on day five as day one.

items.t: The one thing everybody agrees on about body weight
items.d: Whether the pills work less well at higher body weights is genuinely contested — one US label mentions it only as a subgroup buried in its clinical studies rather than as a warning, and the European regulator reviewed the same evidence back in 2014 and deleted its weight statements outright, and the study behind the numbers people quote was small. What is not contested: the copper IUD's effectiveness does not vary with body weight.
items.note: If levonorgestrel is what you can actually get hold of, take it. Taking it beats not taking it.

items.t: Two things that stop it working
items.d: Two different kinds of morning-after pill within five days of each other can cancel each other out. And enzyme-inducing medicines reduce it: rifampin, St. John's wort, carbamazepine, phenytoin, topiramate and some HIV medicines.
items.note: There is no evidence that recreational drugs affect it either way, because nobody has studied it. The documented risk is prescribed medicines and St. John's wort, which is sold over the counter.

sources.name: EMA — levonorgestrel and ulipristal remain suitable regardless of bodyweight (2014)

interactions.headline: The combinations that put people in the hospital

items.t: Poppers and erection pills
items.d: Both drop blood pressure, and together they can drop it catastrophically. The FDA labels contraindicate nitrites outright. After tadalafil (Cialis) allow at least 48 hours. After sildenafil (Viagra) the label says the safe interval is unknown, even at 24 hours.
items.note: Swallowing poppers rather than inhaling is a hospital emergency, not something to sleep off — it turns blood brown and starves it of oxygen. Blue or gray lips with breathlessness after someone drank from a small bottle is a 911 call.

items.t: Boosted HIV medication and MDMA
items.d: If your regimen contains ritonavir or cobicistat, it slows how your body clears MDMA — one clinician guide puts it at five to ten times, and says avoid. The evidence is case reports rather than trials, but one of them was fatal and another nearly so.
items.note: Look at what you actually take. Boosters are in darunavir, atazanavir, Kaletra, Stribild, Genvoya, Symtuza, Prezcobix and Evotaz. Bictegravir and dolutegravir regimens without a booster do not do this.

sources.name: NY/NJ AIDS Education and Training Center — recreational drugs and antiretrovirals

items.t: GHB and GBL — the margin is the problem
items.d: The dose that gives the effect people want and the dose that stops breathing are only about five times apart, in a drug usually measured by eye from a squeeze bottle. Alcohol narrows that further and was involved in 76% of GHB emergency visits. There is no antidote — treatment is keeping the airway open.
items.note: GBL can be two to three times stronger than GHB by volume, so swapping one for the other at the same amount is an overdose. A marked oral syringe measures it; two hours is the usual gap before redosing. Alcohol, benzos, ketamine and meth stack with it — the depressant effects add up, and that combination is where most GHB overdoses come from. Withdrawal from regular use can start within hours of the last dose and bring on seizures and delirium that need a hospital — do not stop abruptly alone.

testing.headline: Getting tested
testing.blurb: Free testing exists in most of the country, and the part people get wrong is not where — it is when.

items.t: Testing too early tells you about last year, not last week
items.b: Every test has a window: the gap between an exposure and the point the test can see it. Test three days after a risk and a negative is real information about everything BEFORE that exposure and says nothing at all about it. For HIV: a lab nucleic-acid test can find it 10 to 33 days after, a lab antigen/antibody test 18 to 45 days, and a rapid finger-stick or at-home antibody test 23 to 90 days. The faster the result, the longer the window.

items.t: Which test you get is not the same question as how fast you get it
items.b: An at-home antibody test is the slowest to close its window and the easiest to actually do. A clinic drawing blood from a vein closes it soonest. If something happened recently, the useful move is often to test now for a baseline and again after the window, rather than picking one moment and hoping.

items.t: Free is normal, not a favor
items.b: Health departments, Planned Parenthood, syringe service programs, and many community clinics test at no cost, and a lot of them do not ask for insurance or an ID. Mail-in kits exist too. None of it is conditional on stopping using.

items.t: If you inject, ask for hepatitis C as well
items.b: It is not on a standard STI panel and has to be asked for. It transmits through shared equipment far more readily than through sex, and the app's other pages assume the injecting route rather than this one.

sources.name: CDC — HIV testing and window periods
CDC — find free and low-cost testing near you

after.headline: After a positive result
after.blurb: Most of what people fear here is either fixable or already over by the time they are told.

items.t: Chlamydia, gonorrhea and syphilis are cured with antibiotics
items.b: Not managed — cured. Treatment is usually a single injection or a short course. What matters afterwards is not having sex until treatment is finished and any partner is treated too, or you hand it back and forth.

items.t: Get retested at three months, not to check the cure
items.b: CDC advises retesting about three months after treatment for chlamydia or gonorrhea. That is not doubt about whether the antibiotics worked — reinfection from an untreated partner is common, and it is the most likely thing a follow-up finds.

items.t: You can tell a partner without telling them who you are
items.b: Health departments run partner services that will notify someone anonymously, and free sites will send an anonymous text or email for you. Nobody has to hear it from you directly for them to get treated.

items.t: Hepatitis C is curable, and using is not a reason to be refused
items.b: Eight to twelve weeks of tablets cure well over ninety per cent of cases. The joint AASLD and IDSA guidance is explicit that ongoing substance use is not a reason to withhold treatment, and studies of people actively injecting show high completion and cure rates. If a provider says you have to be abstinent first, that is their policy, not the standard of care.

items.t: HIV is treatable and treatment stops transmission
items.b: Someone on treatment with an undetectable viral load does not transmit HIV sexually. That is a settled finding, not an optimistic framing.

sources.name: AASLD/IDSA — HCV guidance: treat regardless of ongoing substance use
CDC — HIV testing and window periods

doxypep.headline: Doxy-PEP
doxypep.blurb: An antibiotic taken after sex to prevent bacterial STIs. Newer than most of this page, and not for everyone.

items.t: What it is
items.b: A single 200 mg dose of doxycycline taken within 72 hours after oral, vaginal or anal sex — no more than 200 mg in any 24 hours. In trials it cut syphilis and chlamydia by more than seventy per cent and gonorrhea by roughly half.

items.t: Who CDC recommends it for
items.b: Men who have sex with men, and transgender women, who have had syphilis, chlamydia or gonorrhea diagnosed in the past twelve months. That is the group the evidence covers.

items.t: Who it is not established for
items.b: Trials in cisgender women have not shown the same benefit, and there is not enough evidence for heterosexual men. That is an absence of proof rather than proof it does not work — it means the honest answer is a conversation with a prescriber, not this page.

items.t: It is prescribed, and it is not a substitute
items.b: You need a prescription, and it does nothing for HIV — PrEP is a separate thing that does that job. Doxycycline also makes some people burn more easily in the sun.

sources.name: CDC — Clinical guidelines on doxycycline postexposure prophylaxis, 2024

sitting.note: HAND-WRITTEN. Peer support for someone having a hard time on a drug — NOT overdose response. The boundary between the two is the most important thing in this file and is stated first, in a stop callout, because sitting with someone who actually needs an ambulance is how a survivable night becomes a death. Zendo's four principles are used with attribution; Fireside's number verified 2026-08-11.
sitting.headline: Sitting with someone having a hard time
sitting.intro: Most difficult experiences do not need a hospital. They need one calm person who stays. This is what that person actually does.

notThis.title: First: is this a hard time, or an emergency?
notThis.body: Stop reading and call 911 if any of these is true.
notThis.detail: None of what follows applies to any of that. Sitting with someone is for fear, confusion, panic and overwhelm — not for a body that is failing.
signs: Breathing is slow, stopped, or sounds like snoring or gurgling
Their skin is blue or gray
A seizure that does not stop, or a second one
Their body is very hot to touch and they are confused

principles.title: The four principles
principles.credit: From the Zendo Project, who have used this model with over 1,900 people at festivals and events since 2012.

items.name: Create a safe space
items.what: Somewhere quieter and dimmer than where they are now, with fewer people. Ask before you move them or touch them. Sit at their level rather than standing over them. Deal with the obvious physical things — water, a blanket, somewhere to sit down, a route to a bathroom.

items.name: Sit, don't guide
items.what: You are not steering the experience. Words often get in the way, so use fewer than feels natural. Do not analyze what is happening to them or explain what it means. Listen, and let silence be allowed.

items.name: Talk through, not down
items.what: Do not try to pull someone out of what they are feeling — help them go through it. "Tell me about it" beats "you're fine". Reassurance that dismisses the experience tends to make someone feel more alone in it, not less.

items.name: Difficult is not the same as bad
items.what: Frightening and painful experiences are not automatically harmful ones, and the way somebody is met while it happens changes how it lands afterwards. Panic in the room makes it worse; steadiness makes it survivable.

sources.name: Zendo Project — working with difficult psychedelic experiences

doing.title: What that looks like in practice

items.t: Say who you are, more than once.
items.b: Time and identity get slippery. "I'm Sam, we're at my place, you took something and it's making you feel strange, I'm staying with you" — repeated calmly whenever they need it — does more work than anything clever.

items.t: Give the feeling a shape and an end.
items.b: "This is the drug, and it will pass" is true, orienting, and worth saying often. If you know roughly how long the substance lasts, saying so helps.

items.t: Breathe with them, don't instruct them.
items.b: Sit close and slow your own breathing. People match it without being told. "Breathe!" as a command mostly reads as alarm.

items.t: Offer, never impose.
items.b: Water, a different room, a blanket, the lights lower, going outside. Ask; accept no. Someone who has lost their footing needs to be the one still making choices.

items.t: Keep your own face calm.
items.b: In an altered state people read expressions far more than sentences. If you look frightened, they will believe there is something to be frightened of.

items.t: Stay until it is over, and a while after.
items.b: The tail is where people are left alone. It is also when they are most likely to want to talk.

items.t: Don't argue with what they are seeing or feeling.
items.b: You cannot win, and trying makes you an opponent instead of an anchor.

items.t: Don't crowd them.
items.b: A ring of concerned faces reads as an audience or a threat. One or two people, maximum.

items.t: Don't give them more drugs to fix it.
items.b: Including alcohol and including a benzodiazepine that is not theirs. It adds an unknown to a situation that already has too many.

items.t: Don't threaten them with hospital or police to get compliance.
items.b: It escalates fear at the exact moment fear is the problem — and it teaches them not to tell anyone next time.

items.t: Don't leave them alone to "sleep it off".
items.b: This is the single most common way a hard time turns into an emergency nobody witnessed.

items.t: Don't make it about how worried you were.
items.b: That conversation is legitimate, and it belongs to a later day.

overamping.title: If it's a stimulant, not a psychedelic
overamping.body: Overamping — too much stimulant — looks different: racing heart, chest tightness, overheating, paranoia, jaw clenching, hours without sleep. The sitting principles still apply, and a few physical things matter more: get them somewhere cool, keep water going in small amounts rather than large, and get them off their feet.
overamping.warn: Overheating is the part that becomes medical. A body that is very hot, with confusion, is an emergency — not something to sit through.

lines.name: Fireside Project
lines.what: Free peer support by phone or text, during or after a psychedelic experience. Anonymous. You can hand them the phone.

lines.name: Never Use Alone
lines.what: Stays on the line and sends help if someone stops responding. For opioids, not psychedelics.

lines.name: Poison Control
lines.what: Free, 24/7, confidential. They answer "is this dangerous" questions without involving police.

after.title: Afterwards
after.body: Let them sleep, and check on them the next day. A difficult experience someone was accompanied through often settles into something they can make sense of; the same experience gone through alone tends not to. If they want to talk about it, listening is still the whole job — you do not need to interpret it for them.

stimulants.note: Hand-curated. Sleep loss and psychosis are covered together because they arrive together. Where the evidence cannot separate the drug from the sleep, the page says so rather than picking one.
stimulants.headline: Staying up, and coming down
stimulants.blurb: What days without sleep do on their own, what stimulant psychosis actually looks like, how to help somebody in it, and what it costs to call for help.

sleep.headline: What being awake does by itself
sleep.lead: None of the studies below involved drugs. This is what sleep loss alone does to a healthy person.

items.t: Hours awake convert into something like being drunk
items.d: Forty people were kept awake 28 hours in one condition and given alcohol in another. After 17 hours awake, performance matched a blood alcohol level of 0.05%. After 24 hours awake, it matched roughly 0.10% — over the legal limit everywhere in the US. A second study of 39 people found the same thing independently.
items.note: This is not about willpower. The impairment happens whether or not you feel impaired.

items.t: You stop being able to tell
items.d: In 48 adults held to restricted sleep for two weeks, the people on six hours and the people on four hours rated their own sleepiness about the same — while their actual performance kept diverging. Self-assessment is the first thing to go.

items.t: Everything gets bigger
items.d: After about 35 hours awake, the brain's threat center responded roughly 60% more strongly to unpleasant images, with the connection to the part that normally regulates it weakened. Small things stop feeling small. That is measurable, not a character flaw.

hallucination.headline: Sleep loss alone will do this eventually
hallucination.lead: A review of 21 studies covering 760 people, all of them healthy, none of them on drugs, found a consistent timeline.

stages.d: Perceptual distortions, anxiety, irritability, feeling detached from yourself, losing track of time.
Delusions. At this point the review describes the picture as resembling acute psychosis.

body: Vision is affected most often, then touch, then hearing. It happened in 20 of the 21 studies — but how many people it happens to varies enormously, from about 1 in 9 in one large study of army recruits at 112 hours awake, to everyone in some smaller ones.
It is worst around 4am. Time awake matters, but so does what time it is.
Recovery took roughly half as long as the time spent awake. Most people were fine after sleeping. In five of the studies, some people were still confused or having odd thoughts days or weeks later.
hallucination.note: So: if you have been up three days and things are getting strange, that is not necessarily the drug, and it is not you going mad permanently. It is a documented effect of not sleeping, and sleep is the treatment.

sources.name: Waters et al., Frontiers in Psychiatry 2018 (21 studies, 760 people)

interaction.headline: Sleep loss and stimulants together — what is actually known
body: This is where honest reporting matters, because the obvious answer is not the proven one.

Sleep loss alone produces psychosis-like states in drug-free volunteers. That is solid. Methamphetamine alone produces psychotic symptoms in a dose-dependent way — in 278 people tracked across more than a thousand months, symptoms were present in 25% of months, and the odds rose sharply with days of use in that month. That is also solid.

What nobody has cleanly shown is the two multiplying. The one study that compared people who developed amphetamine psychosis with people who used and did not found the psychosis group had been awake longer — but they had also used more, and no study separates those. A systematic review of risk factors found only frequency of use and dependence severity consistently associated with psychosis; sleep deprivation was not established as independent.
interaction.note: We are telling you this because sleep is one of the few things in reach. Treat it as worth protecting, not as a proven cause you can point at afterwards.

sources.name: McKetin et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2013 (278 people, 1,064 person-months)
Arunogiri et al., Aust N Z J Psychiatry 2018 (systematic review)

items.t: Mostly it is being certain someone is after you
items.d: Across several inpatient studies, persecutory delusions were the most common feature — 77% of 168 people in one, 85% of 152 in another. Hearing things came next, in roughly half. Seeing things was less common, and feeling things on the skin was rarer than the “meth mites” stories suggest: in the study that counted it, 2 of 152.

items.t: Most of it passes quickly
items.d: Of 205 emergency department presentations with psychotic features, 170 resolved completely, 200 were handled without admission, and the median stay was 15 hours. In people sick enough to be admitted to a psychiatric ward it takes longer — of 152 inpatients, about 1 in 3 had not recovered within a month.
items.note: Which of those two pictures applies to you depends mostly on how bad it is when somebody looks at you, not on the drug.

items.t: It can be the first sign of something else
items.d: Across a meta-analysis of 50 studies covering 40,783 people, about 22% of amphetamine-induced psychoses were later diagnosed as schizophrenia. But a Swedish study of 7,606 people found the ones who converted were marked by inherited risk for psychosis — not by heavier drug use. Their conclusion was that this is a drug-precipitated illness in people already vulnerable, rather than one the drug creates from nothing.
items.note: Worth knowing in both directions: it does not mean you are destined for schizophrenia, and it does mean a first episode is worth telling a doctor about.

helping.headline: Helping somebody who is in it
helping.lead: This is consensus guidance from emergency psychiatry, and the people who wrote it say plainly that the evidence base is thin. It is still the best there is, and most of it costs nothing.

items.t: One person talks
items.d: Not three. Several people talking at once is one of the reliable ways to make it worse. Everyone else steps back.

items.t: Two arms' length, hands visible
items.d: Stay far enough away that neither of you feels cornered, and make sure you can both leave. Stand at an angle rather than squared up. If they tell you to move, move immediately.

items.t: Short sentences, then wait
items.d: Simple words, one idea at a time, and leave a gap. Processing is slow right now.

items.t: Do not argue with the content
items.d: You do not have to agree that it is true, and you must not pretend to. What works is agreeing that they are experiencing it: you have never been through what they are going through, and you believe that they are going through it.

items.t: Offer real choices
items.d: A blanket, water, somewhere quieter, a phone call. Choice is the only power somebody has when they feel cornered — but only offer what you can actually deliver. Never promise something to calm them down that you cannot produce.

emergency.title: When it stops being a psychological emergency and becomes a medical one
emergency.body: Get help immediately for: a temperature you would call dangerous, confusion or unconsciousness, chest pain, a seizure, or a stroke sign. Overheating is the one on that list people die of, and it moves fastest — a body cannot stay that hot for long. Call 911, and cool them while you wait — cold water over as much skin as you can get to, re-wet constantly, with air moving over it. Not a cloth on the forehead. See Heat and water for the whole sequence.

sources.name: Richmond et al., Project BETA verbal de-escalation, West J Emerg Med 2012
National Harm Reduction Coalition — responding to overamping

calling.headline: What calling for help actually costs
calling.lead: We are not going to tell you it is simple. Here is what the numbers say, so you can decide.

items.d: Emergency services were dispatched in about 2 in 100 calls. Across nearly two million calls, dispatch happened in about half of the calls where the counselor judged someone to be at imminent risk. Roughly half of those dispatches were without the person's agreement.

sources.name: Vibrant Emotional Health — imminent risk data

items.t: 911 for a stimulant overdose
items.d: In one large US city across two years, 21% of stimulant-involved overdose responses were followed by the person being jailed within six hours — against 9% for opioid-involved ones. That is one city, and it is the only measurement of its kind we could find.

sources.name: Ray et al., Drug Alcohol Depend 2022

items.t: Good Samaritan laws do not cover this
items.d: All 50 states and DC have them now — Wyoming was the last, in 2025 — but they are written for drug overdose, not for psychiatric crisis. They mostly do not cover outstanding warrants, and they generally protect against minor drug charges only.
items.note: Nobody has ever studied what happens when someone calls for help specifically for drug-induced psychosis. We are naming that gap rather than filling it with reassurance.

sources.name: Network for Public Health Law — overdose Good Samaritan laws

calling.note: None of this is a reason to let somebody overheat or stop breathing. It is a reason to know what you are choosing, and to make the call anyway when it is that kind of emergency.

items.t: The shape of it
items.d: Across three small inpatient studies, the worst is in the first 24 hours and eases over roughly the first week, with a longer tail of at least a couple more weeks. Depression and psychotic symptoms tend to lift within about a week. Anxiety and craving do not follow that curve — craving in one study did not drop until the second week.
items.note: Those studies were all in supervised settings with a bed and food. Crashing alone is harder than the numbers suggest.

items.t: Nothing you can take makes it shorter
items.d: A Cochrane review found four randomized trials with 125 people between them and concluded no medication is effective for amphetamine withdrawal. There is no evidence for melatonin, for antihistamines, or for benzodiazepines here.
items.note: Benzodiazepines carry a specific risk worth stating: fentanyl does turn up in the stimulant supply — in samples tested it has run around 6 to 15% for powder cocaine and powder meth, and under 2% for crack and crystal — and combining a benzodiazepine with an opioid is how people stop breathing. And stopping benzodiazepines abruptly after regular use can itself be dangerous.

items.t: Water is not an antidote
items.d: Thirst is a better guide here than a schedule, and about two to three cups an hour counting everything is the ceiling your kidneys can clear. Stimulants and MDMA both stop your body clearing water properly, and every year people drink far past that believing it will fix a bad experience and swell their brain — a splitting headache, confusion and vomiting are the early signs. Food is what keeps your electrolytes where they should be.

sources.name: Hew-Butler et al. — 3rd International Exercise-Associated Hyponatremia Consensus (2015)
Atila et al., JAMA Netw Open 2024 — MDMA and hyponatremia

supervision.note: Hand-curated. Nothing here explains how to beat a test — that is out of scope on purpose. This is about understanding what you are facing and what you are actually entitled to.
supervision.headline: Drug testing, probation and parole
supervision.blurb: What a test can and cannot see, what to do when it says something wrong, and what the law says about being on methadone or buprenorphine while under supervision.

rights.headline: A positive screen is not a result yet
body: Almost every test starts as an immunoassay — a fast, cheap, presumptive screen. It is not an identification. It reacts to a shape, which is why it can be set off by things you did not take and miss things you did.
The confirmation is a different machine: GC/MS or LC-MS/MS, which identifies the actual molecule. Labs do not always run it unless somebody asks.

callout.title: On federal supervision, contesting it is what triggers confirmation
callout.body: Federal law requires a confirmed result before a screen can cost you your liberty, and the courts' own guide says that when an instant screening result is positive and contested by the person under supervision, the sample must be sent for GC/MS confirmation. The trigger is you saying you dispute it. Say it immediately, say it plainly, and ask for it in writing.

rights.caveat: This is federal supervision. State probation and parole rules vary and we have not verified them state by state — ask your attorney or public defender what your state requires, and ask before you need it.

panels.headline: What is actually on the test
panels.blurb: A panel only finds what it was built to look for. Several of the drugs most present in the supply are on no routine panel at all.

items.t: Fentanyl is not on a classic 5-panel
items.d: The standard five — amphetamines, cocaine, cannabis, opiates, PCP — does not include it. Fentanyl has no structural resemblance to morphine, so morphine-calibrated opiate assays do not react to it. It needs its own assay. Federal agency testing added a dedicated fentanyl line effective July 7 2025; DOT-regulated testing still has not, as of August 2026.

items.t: Xylazine is on nothing routine
items.d: Absent from both federal panels. A dedicated xylazine immunoassay exists but is labeled for forensic use, not clinical. If somebody wants to know whether xylazine is involved, it has to be asked for specifically.

items.t: Methadone and buprenorphine need their own assays
items.d: Neither is on the federal panel and neither cross-reacts with the opiate screen. Being prescribed one does not make you show up positive for opioids, and a routine panel will not confirm you are taking it either.

items.t: Gabapentin, kratom and most novel benzos are invisible by default
items.d: None are on the federal panel. Novel benzodiazepines are assay-dependent — a benzodiazepine screen will often flag etizolam or flualprazolam, sometimes at several times the sensitivity of its own calibrator, but a negative screen does not rule out bromazolam. Which ones get caught depends on the manufacturer's platform.

sources.name: Federal Register 91 FR 12308 — current HHS testing cutoffs (March 13 2026)

windows.headline: How long it stays in you
windows.blurb: Urine, because that is what almost every test uses. Every figure carries the study it came from — a window without its conditions is not a fact.
windows.lead: Three things decide the answer far more than the drug does: how much and how long you have been using, what threshold the lab set, and which machine they ran. The same drug can give wildly different answers on all three.

method.title: The method matters more than most people are told
method.body: Eighteen people were given one 0.4 mg dose of buprenorphine. On the immunoassay it was detectable for a mean of 9 hours. On LC-MS/MS, from the identical dose in the same people, a mean of 76 hours. Its metabolite was still positive in every single person when the study ended at 96 hours. Same drug, same dose, same bodies — the machine set the window.

sources.name: Kronstrand et al., J Anal Toxicol 2008 (N=18)

rows.urine: Roughly half a day to 5½ days for fentanyl itself; its metabolite norfentanyl ran 2.7 to 10.7 days. A separate group of 12 people entering treatment averaged 7.3 days for fentanyl and 13.3 for norfentanyl — one person was still positive at 19 and 26 days.
rows.note: Far longer than the two to four days people expect from short-acting opioids. If you are being tested after switching off fentanyl, this is the number to know.

rows.urine: The heroin-specific marker (6-MAM) is gone fast — often within 8 hours. Morphine itself is 1 to 3 days for occasional use; in 52 chronic users the average was 4.95 days and the longest 11.3 days at a sensitive cutoff.
1 to 14 days. Many methadone assays detect only the parent drug and not its metabolite EDDP — which is why EDDP testing is what distinguishes actually taking it from a sample it was added to.
4 to 24 hours by immunoassay; 23 to 96 hours by mass spectrometry. See above — the difference is the machine, not you.
Short-acting ones around 3 days. Long-acting, in chronic use, up to 30 days. Alprazolam runs 1 to 5 days and clonazepam 1 to 12.
rows.note: But see the section above: alprazolam, lorazepam and clonazepam frequently do not show up at all on a standard screen, whatever the window.

rows.urine: Measured as its metabolite. In 18 chronic users during monitored cessation the average last positive was 57.5 hours, with the longest at 147 hours — a little over 6 days.
Highly cutoff-dependent. In controlled dosing, dropping to the lower of two common thresholds extended detection by up to 24 hours for methamphetamine and up to 34 hours overall.
rows.note: Prescribed amphetamine can sometimes be distinguished from illicit by testing which mirror-image form is present, but we could not verify any specific threshold a lab uses to make that call — do not assume it will be done.

rows.urine: The widest range of anything here, and the most cutoff-dependent. The same frequent users in one study were positive for 17, 22 or 27 days depending purely on which of three thresholds was applied. In 60 people on a closed unit, grouped by starting concentration, the average last positive was 4.3, 9.7 or 15.4 days.
rows.note: Published maximums are floors, not ceilings — several of these studies ended while people were still testing positive.

rows.urine: Its metabolite norketamine was detectable up to 14 days by the most sensitive method in one hospital study, and ketamine itself up to 11 days. One child in that study never tested positive at all across 16 days.
40 to 130 hours to fall below a common cutoff, median 78, in 32 people in detox. But see hand sanitizer above — EtG at these thresholds does not distinguish drinking from incidental exposure.
Roughly half a day to 5 days in urine. Not on any routine panel, so it will only be found if someone specifically looks.
1 to 2 days. Not on the federal panel.

gaps.title: What we could not verify, and are not going to guess
items: MDMA. We found no controlled-dosing source we could actually read, in any matrix. Rather than repeat a number off a rehab marketing page, there is nothing here.
Blood, saliva and hair windows for most of these drugs. Urine is well studied; the others largely are not, and the tables that circulate for them are mostly unsourced.
Kratom, and most novel benzodiazepines. No commercial cutoffs we could confirm at source.

sources.name: Bird et al., Am J Addict 2025 — fentanyl and xylazine urine windows
Huhn et al., Drug Alcohol Depend 2020 — fentanyl in treatment entry
Preston et al., J Anal Toxicol 2002 — cocaine during cessation
Oyler et al., Clin Chem 2002 — methamphetamine controlled dosing
Adamowicz & Kala, J Anal Toxicol 2005 — ketamine
Helander et al., Alcohol Alcohol 2009 — urinary EtG
ARUP Consult — drug half-lives and urine detection windows

windows.perDrugNote: Urine, and only as a range — how much you used, for how long, which threshold the lab set and which machine they ran all move this more than the drug does.

misreads.headline: When the test is wrong
misreads.blurb: Both directions happen, and both are documented.

items.t: Hand sanitizer can produce a positive alcohol test
items.d: In a study of 11 people using ethanol hand sanitizer through the day for three days and drinking nothing, urine EtG reached 2,001 ng/mL — four times the cutoff most labs use, and twenty times the sensitive clinical one. The authors concluded plainly that current EtG cutoffs do not distinguish drinking from incidental exposure. A useful tell: EtG went high while EtS stayed low.

sources.name: Reisfield et al., J Anal Toxicol 2011

items.t: Your prescribed benzodiazepine may not show up
items.d: Most benzodiazepine immunoassays are built around oxazepam or nordiazepam. Alprazolam and lorazepam are excreted mainly as glucuronides and are not detected unless the lab does an extra hydrolysis step, which most do not. Clonazepam becomes 7-aminoclonazepam, which barely cross-reacts. A negative screen is not evidence you stopped taking what you were prescribed.

sources.name: Moeller et al., Mayo Clin Proc 2017

items.t: Ordinary medicines set off the methadone screen
items.d: Verapamil, diphenhydramine and doxylamine are documented causes of methadone false positives. Diphenhydramine is Benadryl; doxylamine is in night-time cold medicine and some sleep aids.

sources.name: Moeller et al., Mayo Clin Proc 2017

cannabis.headline: Testing negative then positive is a known pattern
body: This is the one most likely to be used against you, and it is the one most people cannot argue their way out of without knowing it.

Cannabis does not leave the body on a smooth downward curve. Under strictly supervised abstinence — where continued use was ruled out by the study design — people alternated between positive and negative results for weeks. In a study of 60 people on a closed research unit, 40% did not reach their peak concentration until up to 2.9 days AFTER abstinence began.
So a negative followed by a positive is a documented excretion pattern in people who have not used. It is not proof of anything.

How long you stay positive depends enormously on the cutoff, which is why any single number is close to meaningless without one attached. The same frequent users in the same study were positive for 17 days at one threshold, 22 at a lower one, and 27 at a lower one still.
cannabis.note: Most chronic users clear faster than the famous long-tail figures suggest — but in one study of 37 people, roughly one in four were still above the cutoff after two weeks. Both things are true.

sources.name: Goodwin et al., J Anal Toxicol 2008 (N=60, 6,158 specimens)
Smith-Kielland et al., J Anal Toxicol 1999
Ellis et al., Clin Pharmacol Ther 1985 (N=86, supervised abstinence)

medication.headline: They cannot make you stop your medication
body: If you are prescribed methadone or buprenorphine, a court, a probation officer, a drug court or a jail telling you to taper off it is on very weak legal ground.

Federal law says so directly: medication taken under the supervision of a licensed health care professional is not “illegal use of drugs”. That is the statute, not a guideline — and the Americans with Disabilities Act covers courts, prisons and jails.

This has been enforced. The Justice Department settled with Pennsylvania's court system in January 2024 over exactly this, and with the Massachusetts Parole Board in 2021 over a person being pushed onto a different medication than the one that was working.

callout.title: If it is happening to you
callout.body: Get it in writing if you can — an order, a condition sheet, a message. Then contact a disability rights organization or your public defender. The Legal Action Center works on exactly this and keeps a list of the cases. Tapering because you were told to is the option with the most risk in it — stopping medication is the single largest overdose risk there is, and the order is on weak legal ground to begin with.

medication.caveat: The Justice Department's guidance document says on its face that it does not carry the force of law. The statute it rests on does. Cite the statute.

links.name: DOJ — the ADA and people in treatment for opioid use disorder

sources.name: 42 U.S.C. § 12210(d) — medication under supervision is not illegal use

violations.headline: What a violation actually is
violations.blurb: Most people sent back are not sent back for a new crime.

items.t: Technical violations are the bulk of it
items.d: In 2021, 44% of state prison admissions came from violations of probation or parole — and technical violations alone, things like a missed appointment with a supervision officer or a failed drug test, account for nearly a quarter of every admission to state prison. Not a new offense. A quarter.

sources.name: CSG Justice Center — Confined and Costly (2021 admissions data)

items.t: Calling 911 may not protect you from a violation
items.d: 27 states and DC extend Good Samaritan protection to probation and parole violations. 23 do not. And in Minnesota and North Carolina the statutes expressly preserve the authority to drug test you anyway — meaning the call itself is protected but the test that follows it is not. That is a real trap and worth knowing before the night it matters.

reentry.headline: The first two weeks after release are the most dangerous
body: Tolerance falls fast during any break in use, and jail or prison is a break in use. The dose that was normal before is not normal now.

In a study following 30,237 people released from Washington State prisons, the risk of fatal overdose in the first two weeks after release was 129 times that of the general population. A later North Carolina study, covering 2016 to 2018, found overdose deaths in the first two weeks after release at 46.6 times the expected rate.
The three things those numbers turn on are naloxone in hand on day one, somebody else in the room, and an amount well below what used to be normal — tolerance is what changed, not the drug.

sources.name: Binswanger et al., N Engl J Med 2007
Ranapurwala et al., Am J Public Health 2022

hair.headline: If they use a hair test
body: Hair testing has problems the government's own proposed rule concedes.

It cannot see recent use at all — drugs do not appear in hair for 5 to 7 days after they are taken. And the first centimeter of hair does not represent the last month: because of the time it takes hair to reach the surface, it represents roughly one to two months ago.

A federal proposal published in September 2020 — still not finalized six years later, so it binds nobody today — would not let a hair result stand alone. An agency choosing to test hair must also collect another specimen type, and the rule cites litigation warning that action taken on a hair test alone may be legally vulnerable.

bias.title: It is not the same test for everyone
bias.body: In a study where 44 people took an identical controlled dose of codeine, the amount ending up in their hair tracked hair melanin — the correlation explained about 73% of the variance. Concentrations in black hair were around seven times those in brown and fourteen to fifteen times those in blond. At the cutoff the government proposes, 100% of the black-haired subjects would have been reported positive and only half of the brown-haired ones. Same drug, same dose, different hair.

sources.name: Rollins et al., J Anal Toxicol 2003 (N=44)

hair.thc: One more: finding cannabis metabolites in hair does not prove someone used cannabis. A controlled dosing study found them in hair segments that had already grown before the person ever took any, and in people who had not used at all — transferred by hand, sweat and smoke from someone who had.

sources.name: HHS proposed hair testing guidelines, 85 FR 56108

support.reviewNote: Tone here matters more than completeness. This sits inside a harm reduction tool: it is for someone curious about options, never a push to quit, and never a judgment on anyone still using. Nothing should read as a condition for deserving help. Every link and phone number was verified 2026-08-10 — see EVIDENCE.md for what was checked and what was rejected.

body: Maybe you want to stop. Maybe you want to use less, or more safely. Maybe you want to keep using and just feel like a person again for a while. Maybe the thing you actually need help with is underneath all of it. Every one of those counts, and none of them is the wrong reason to be reading this.
You don’t have to be done using to ask for any of it. You don’t have to be sure, or have a plan, or have anything to show for the last six months.
framing.close: Nothing on this page is a judgment on how you’re living.

underneath.headline: What is often underneath
body: For a lot of people, substance use is not the first thing that happened. It is the thing that made something else survivable.

That is not an excuse and it is not a diagnosis — it is a pattern common enough that the research on it is unambiguous, and it means the useful question is often not “how do I stop” but “what am I carrying, and what would help me put it down”.
underneath.note: Support for that exists separately from anything to do with drugs, and you can go looking for it without ever discussing your use.

options.intro: There are three medications for opioid use disorder. They are treatment, not a substitute addiction, and being on one is not a lesser kind of recovery.

medications.name: Buprenorphine (Suboxone, Sublocade)
medications.what: A partial opioid agonist. It has a ceiling effect, which is why it carries a much lower overdose risk than the opioids it replaces.
medications.how: Any clinician with a normal DEA registration can prescribe it — a regular doctor, a clinic, a community health center, telehealth, or an emergency room. It is filled at an ordinary pharmacy. The old special waiver was abolished in 2023 and there is no longer any cap on how many patients a prescriber can treat.
medications.note: Usually started when you are already in mild withdrawal, to avoid precipitated withdrawal. Ask about low-dose initiation if that is a barrier for you.

medications.name: Methadone
medications.what: A full agonist, long acting, and the most studied of the three. It works for many people for whom buprenorphine does not.
medications.how: Only through a licensed opioid treatment program — that restriction is federal law, not a medical judgment about you. Find one through SAMHSA's directory below.
medications.note: Take-home rules loosened permanently in 2024: up to 7 days of take-homes in the first two weeks, up to 14 through the first month, and up to 28 days after that, based on your clinician's judgment rather than a fixed checklist. The old requirement to have used opioids for a year before being admitted is gone.

medications.name: Naltrexone (Vivitrol)
medications.what: A blocker rather than an opioid. Monthly injection or daily pill. Any prescriber can order it.
medications.how: Requires being fully off opioids for roughly 7 to 10 days first.
medications.note: That gap is a real barrier and a real risk — tolerance drops during it, so a return to use in that window is more dangerous than usual. Worth weighing honestly against the other two.

evidence.body: A review of 15 trials and 36 studies covering more than 700,000 people found that while someone is on methadone or buprenorphine, overdose deaths and deaths from all causes drop sharply. In the four weeks after stopping, all-cause mortality was around six times higher, and stayed roughly double after that. The risk is not in taking the medication. It is in the weeks right after stopping — which is worth knowing if anyone pressures you to taper before you are ready.

stimulants.body: There is no approved medication for methamphetamine or cocaine use disorder. The approach with by far the strongest evidence is contingency management — structured, modest rewards for meeting goals you agreed to. It is mostly funded through state Medicaid programs, so availability depends on where you live; California, Delaware, Hawaii, Montana and Washington had approved programs as of early 2025 and more may have been added since. Ask a local provider or call the SAMHSA line below.

sources.name: SAMHSA TIP 33 — Treatment for Stimulant Use Disorders

getting.intro: Two national front doors, then the routes that work when you have no insurance and no money.

routes.name: SAMHSA National Helpline
routes.what: Free, confidential, 24/7, English and Spanish. They will not ask for your name or personal details — only a ZIP code. If you have no insurance they refer you to state-funded programs and sliding-scale providers. This is the fastest human route to care you can afford.

routes.name: FindTreatment.gov
routes.what: The government's treatment locator. Confidential and anonymous. Filter for medication treatment, payment options, and telehealth.

routes.name: Methadone program directory
routes.what: Methadone is only available through a licensed opioid treatment program. This is the official list.

routes.name: Community health centers
routes.what: Federally funded health centers are required to see you regardless of your ability to pay, on a sliding scale. Many prescribe buprenorphine. No insurance needed.

routes.name: Emergency departments can start you
routes.what: Many hospitals now start buprenorphine in the ER and connect you to a prescriber within a few days. In the programs built for this, treatment is not conditional on insurance, on lab results, or on promising to stop using anything else.
Dial 2-1-1 from anywhere in the US for local free and sliding-scale services — treatment, housing, food, transport.

routes.name: Medicaid
routes.what: There is no open enrollment period for Medicaid — you can apply any day of the year. Coverage rules vary by state, and some states can backdate coverage.

routes.name: If you are pregnant
routes.what: Fear of losing a child keeps many people away from care. A federal Plan of Safe Care is a health plan for you and the baby — it is not automatically a child protective services report. What is actually required varies a lot by state, and is often narrower than hospital practice suggests. This free toolkit covers your rights around drug testing, disclosure, and what happens after birth. Methadone and buprenorphine are the standard of care in pregnancy; being pregnant is not a reason to stop.

lines.name: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline
lines.who: Call, text or chat 988 · Spanish: press 2 · ASL videophone available
lines.dispatch: They may send emergency services. Across nearly two million calls, that happened in about 2 in 100 — but in about half of the calls where the counselor judged someone to be at imminent risk. Roughly half of those dispatches were without the person's agreement.

lines.name: Never Use Alone
lines.who: Peer-run, 24/7. No abstinence requirement, no judgment. They stay on the line and send help if you stop responding.

lines.name: Veterans Crisis Line
lines.who: 988 then press 1, or text 838255. No VA enrollment needed.
lines.dispatch: Routes through 988, which may send emergency services without your agreement.

lines.name: Vet Centers
lines.who: Free, strictly confidential counseling at community storefronts kept separate from VA medical records. Combat, military sexual trauma in any era, and bereavement for families.

lines.name: The Trevor Project
lines.who: LGBTQ+ young people. Call, or text START to 678678.
lines.dispatch: In their own words, they “may need to contact a child welfare agency or emergency service.”

lines.name: Trans Lifeline
lines.who: Staffed by trans and nonbinary peers. Policy against calling police or emergency services without your explicit request.
lines.hours: Monday to Friday, 1pm–9pm Eastern. Closed weekends.

lines.name: StrongHearts Native Helpline
lines.who: For Native and Indigenous people. This is a domestic and sexual violence line — not a drug or overdose line.

lines.name: RAINN
lines.dispatch: In their own words, they are “required by law to report to authorities” in some circumstances.

lines.name: Childhelp
lines.who: Child abuse, including adult survivors. Call or text, 24/7.
lines.dispatch: A mandated-reporting line — they may contact child welfare or emergency services.

lines.name: Crisis Text Line
lines.dispatch: They may contact emergency services. Their policy is not stated in a way we could quote.

lines.name: Partnership to End Addiction
lines.who: Free, human-staffed support for families. Text CONNECT to 55753.

peer.intro: Groups differ enormously, and the differences are not always advertised at the door. The most important one is how a group treats people on medication.
peer.medicationNote: If you are on methadone or buprenorphine, this matters before you walk in. Some rooms will treat you as being in recovery without qualification. Others will not let you share or hold a position. You are entitled to know which is which in advance rather than finding out in front of a room.

groups.name: MARA — Medication-Assisted Recovery Anonymous
groups.what: Built specifically for people on medication. No abstinence requirement, no higher power.
groups.medication: Fully supported. This is the point of the group.

groups.name: SMART Recovery
groups.what: Secular, science-based, uses cognitive-behavioral tools. Your goal can be abstinence, moderation, or harm reduction.
groups.medication: Explicitly supported — SMART endorses legally prescribed addiction and psychiatric medication.

groups.name: LifeRing
groups.what: Secular, abstinence-based, no steps and no higher power.
groups.medication: Explicitly fine — their definition of sobriety carves out medically indicated prescribed medication.

groups.name: All Recovery meetings and recovery community centers
groups.what: Multi-pathway by design — 12-step, secular, medication and harm reduction people in the same room. Find your local recovery community organization and ask for their schedule.

groups.name: Narcotics Anonymous
groups.what: The largest and easiest to find. Abstinence-based and explicitly spiritual, though not tied to a religion.
groups.medication: NA as an organization takes no position on your medication and you are welcome to attend. But NA's own literature says individual groups may limit whether you can share or hold a service position, and warns you may meet strong opinions. NA's own advice is to try several meetings.

groups.name: Recovery Dharma
groups.what: Buddhist-informed, peer-governed, non-theistic — no higher power required. Abstinence is held as an intention.
groups.medication: No published position. Their current FAQ does not mention medication either way, so ask locally rather than assuming.

trauma.intro: You can get help with this without ever discussing drugs, and without deciding anything about your use first.

aces.title: What the research actually says
aces.body: A large study of childhood adversity found a stepwise pattern: the more categories of adversity someone reported, the higher their later risk. People reporting five or more were seven to ten times more likely to report drug problems, addiction, or injection drug use. That is one of the strongest patterns in public health.
aces.caveat: It describes populations, not people. One of the study's own lead authors published a correction warning that the score is being misused as if it were a screening or diagnostic tool. Your score is not a diagnosis, not a prognosis, and not a prediction about your life.

sources.name: Anda et al. — limits and misapplications

approaches.name: Seeking Safety
approaches.what: Present-focused coping skills for trauma and substance use at the same time. Does not require abstinence, and does not require retelling what happened. Worth asking for by name — many programs still make sobriety a condition of trauma treatment.

approaches.name: CPT (Cognitive Processing Therapy)
approaches.what: Around 12 sessions, working on the beliefs that formed afterwards — about blame, safety, and trust. A version exists that does not require a detailed account of the event.

approaches.name: Prolonged Exposure
approaches.what: Gradual, repeated approach to the memory and to avoided situations. Effective and demanding — dropping out is common, and deciding it is not for you is a legitimate choice.

approaches.name: EMDR
approaches.what: Attending to the memory while doing guided eye movements or other bilateral stimulation.

approaches.name: Somatic approaches
approaches.what: Body-based work, often experienced as gentler. Honest caveat: the evidence base is much smaller and earlier than the three above, and it is not among the strongly recommended treatments in current clinical guidelines.

experiences.name: Deciding between treatments
experiences.what: A free, non-commercial tool from the VA that compares trauma treatments side by side. No login, no sales.

experiences.name: Finding a therapist you can afford
experiences.what: Open Path connects uninsured and underinsured people to therapists at reduced rates.

experiences.name: Losing someone to an overdose
experiences.what: GRASP runs free peer groups, in person and online, specifically for people grieving a death from substances. Its sister organization does advocacy and naloxone education.

experiences.name: Losing a child, at any age
experiences.what: The Compassionate Friends is free and secular, with long-running online groups for overdose loss. Often the best option where there is no GRASP chapter.

experiences.name: Families of someone still using
experiences.what: Learn to Cope runs peer meetings for families, most weekdays online, including naloxone training.

experiences.name: Adult survivors of childhood abuse
experiences.what: Free peer-led groups and a free workbook.

experiences.name: Chronic pain, including anyone tapered against their will
experiences.what: The 2022 federal prescribing guideline was written partly to correct the misuse of the 2016 one. It states plainly that its recommendations are not rigid rules and should not lead to rapid tapering or abrupt discontinuation. If you were cut off, that was not what the guideline asked for.

experiences.name: Free self-help that is not a product
experiences.what: PTSD Coach from the VA, usable in a browser with nothing to install and nothing to sign up for. It does not replace care, and says so itself.

cost.headline: If you cannot pay
cost.body: Cost, insurance, immigration status, a record, or no ID stop more people than lack of wanting. Most of these routes have a version that does not require money or paperwork: the SAMHSA line refers to state-funded and sliding-scale programs without asking who you are, community health centers cannot turn you away over money, and Medicaid has no enrollment deadline.
cost.note: Community health centers are required to see people regardless of ability to pay.

supplies.intro: Naloxone, test strips, and safer-use supplies. Free options first, because most people reading this cannot pay and burying them under vendors is its own barrier.

free.name: NEXT Distro
free.what: Free naloxone by mail, discreetly packaged. Their state finder covers every state — where they cannot ship directly they hand you off to a program that can. This is the single best starting point if you are not sure where to look.

free.name: Your state health department
free.what: Many states mail free naloxone to any resident who asks, and some include fentanyl test strips. Which tier your state falls into is below.

free.name: Syringe service programs
free.what: SSPs give out naloxone, test strips, sterile supplies and wound care, usually with no ID and no questions. They are also the most reliable place to hear what is actually circulating locally.

directories.name: Harm Reduction Near You
directories.what: National Harm Reduction Coalition's directory of programs by location.

directories.name: NASEN syringe program directory
directories.what: The national list of syringe service programs.
Dial 2-1-1 and ask for harm reduction supplies or naloxone. Works everywhere, including where nothing above does.

paid.name: Naloxone over the counter
paid.what: Narcan 4 mg and RiVive 3 mg are available without a prescription at pharmacies nationwide. Worth knowing as a fallback, but check the free routes first — you should not have to pay for this.

paid.name: DanceSafe
paid.what: Reagent kits and fentanyl test strips. Their storefront moved to Transparency in March 2026; the strips are still made by the same manufacturer.

paid.name: BTNX
paid.what: The manufacturer of most fentanyl, xylazine, benzodiazepine and nitazene strips used in the US.

byState.intro: What your state offers, as of August 2026. This changes often — if your state is not in the first group, the NEXT Distro finder above still covers you.

tiers.label: Free naloxone AND test strips by mail, to any resident
Free naloxone by mail, no test strips
tiers.note: Some cap how many kits you can request, and Alaska ships only to Alaska addresses.

tiers.label: State program supplies organizations, not individuals
tiers.note: These states fund bulk naloxone for agencies and programs. As an individual, go through NEXT Distro or a local syringe service program instead — the state page will not help you directly.

tiers.label: No verified statewide mail program for individuals
tiers.note: Nonprofits often fill the gap. Hawaii's mail program covers Kauaʻi, Lānaʻi and Molokaʻi only, despite what most sources say.

closed.title: Recently closed — do not rely on these
items: Oklahoma discontinued its mail-order fentanyl test strip program, and the statewide naloxone vending machines were removed in September 2024.
Idaho repealed authorization for syringe service programs; all programs closed on June 30, 2024.
Federal grant funds can no longer be used to buy fentanyl or xylazine test strips as of April 2026, so state-funded strip programs are the most likely of any listing here to disappear.

supplies.legalNote: Fentanyl test strips are legal in most states but not all, and xylazine strips are covered in fewer. Ordering by mail does not change your state's law. See the legality section on the Test tab before you order.

grassroots.intro: Programs run by and for people who use drugs. These often reach people the formal system turns away, ask for no ID and no story, and tend to know what is actually circulating locally weeks before any official alert does. Several also stay stocked when state programs run dry.

items.name: Grassroots Harm Reduction
items.what: A national network supporting local peer-run programs. Often the fastest route to free supplies where no storefront carries them — and they answer on social media when a website would be too slow.

items.name: National Survivors Union
items.what: The national union of drug users and sex workers, organized by people who use drugs — formerly Urban Survivors Union. Methadone advocacy, harm reduction education, an advocacy academy, and support for local and underground syringe programs. If there is no chapter where you are, they help you start one.
items.delivery: Local chapters, plus national online meetings

items.name: Never Use Alone
items.what: Peer-run, 24/7, staffed by people with lived experience. You give a location, they stay on the line, and they send help if you stop responding. No abstinence requirement and no judgment — verified from their own policy.

items.name: SafeSpot
items.what: Another peer-run overdose prevention line, expanding to more states.

items.name: Brave
items.what: Peer-built overdose detection hardware — a button you press when you are about to use alone, and sensors for bathrooms and private rooms, both wired to a responder who checks on you. Sold to organizations rather than individuals, so this is one to ask your local program about.
items.cost: Devices are purchased, not free — configuration fee on a first order.
items.delivery: Devices, installed by a program or building

items.name: Remedy Alliance / For The People
